Are we not allowed to say a genocide began on 7 October, too? Submitted by Barry Malone on Wed, 10/21/2026 - 21:19 Western media commemorate the Israelis killed three years ago, while largely ignoring the genocide that began the same day A girl looks at the temporary tents of displaced Palestinians, alongside destroyed buildings, in Gaza City on 7 October 2026 (Omar al-Qattaa/AFP) Off Just after 4pm local time on 7 October 2023, Al Jazeera’s Youmna El Sayed stood on a rooftop to update her audience on the latest from Gaza City, which was already under bombardment following the Hamas-led attacks on Israel early that same morning. Live on air, as she was about to answer a question from a news anchor, we heard the sound of a missile scream down from the sky before thumping into a tower block with a horrible boom, the orange flash of an explosion appearing over her shoulder. Sayed cried out in shock and ducked from view, but as so many brave Palestinian journalists would do over the next three years, she tried to continue reporting. “We have just witnessed live what an Israeli air raid looks like on a populated area of Gaza City,” said the anchor, Cyril Vanier. “What we believe is a residential building.” That initial strike on Palestine Tower , which indeed was a mixed-use residential and office building, was what the Israelis call a “roof knock” - a warning that a building is about to be destroyed, giving people an absurdly short time to escape. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Minutes later, the rockets intended to obliterate the tower arrived , and about 80 apartments - homes that would have had family photos on the walls, toys on the floor and dishes in the sink - were instantly reduced to a painful memory. Vanier’s words were a portent of what was to come, because what we witnessed in that viral moment has since been repeated daily. Israel’s campaign of extermination against the Palestinian people had begun. The genocide started on 7 October. 'Wicked city' In fact, it started just hours after Hamas and other groups launched their dawn attack. By 8:24am, the Times of Israel reported that Israeli strikes were under way. The Indonesian Hospital in Beit Lahiya was struck a short while after, killing two people, including a member of staff. This set in motion what would become a pattern of attacking medical facilities, doctors, patients and employees: over the next three years, more than 1,700 healthcare workers were killed, many in targeted attacks. Journalist Mohammad al-Salhi was shot dead by Israeli forces in al-Bureij on 7 October, and ambulances were hit outside Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis and in Jabalia, where two paramedics lost their lives and several others were wounded. The industrial-scale slaughter of Palestinian children also began on 7 October. Just after 8pm, with the attack on Gaza ongoing for 12 hours, the Israelis hit a three-storey building in the Zeitoun neighbourhood, where three generations of the al-Dos family lived. Fifteen family members, including seven children , were killed. Adam al-Dos, 18 months old, was the youngest. The entries on Gaza were so fleeting and by-the-numbers that all they did was underline the disparity. They reeked of afterthought Children were also killed in other strikes that day. By 9pm, a provisional death toll of 232 Palestinians was reported . Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other politicians were not shy about making their intentions immediately clear, with intent a key component of legally determining that a genocide has been committed. “We will take mighty vengeance for this black day,” Netanyahu said in a televised address. “We will take revenge for all the young people who lost their lives … We will turn Gaza into a deserted island.” Gaza was “a wicked city”, he added . Yoav Gallant , then the defence minister, vowed to “change reality on the ground in Gaza for the next 50 years”, while Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich reportedly told a cabinet meeting that Israel must “be cruel now and not think too much about the hostages”. An army general made the sinister promise that Hamas had “opened the gates of hell on the Gaza Strip”. All of these statements, and more, were made on 7 October. It is clear that the genocide began that morning. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Hierarchy of suffering Why, then, did much of the western media this month mark the anniversary with wall-to-wall reporting of Israeli commemorations - and only the paltriest of mentions for Palestinians? Why did the BBC run a live blog with pages of stories humanising Israelis killed three years ago, while Palestinians continue to be massacred? Why did the Guardian ? To be clear, it’s not the fact that there was coverage. It’s the immense scale and prominence of it: a scale that amounted to tens of thousands of words and hours of television, yet found little room for Gaza. This highlights the hierarchy of suffering that western media has applied to the events of the last three years. It’s more than a hierarchy of suffering: it’s a hierarchy of peoples. Why Gaza's genocide ranks among the gravest horrors of human history Read More » The BBC’s blog was headlined “Israeli families mourn 7 October victims as memorials held around world”. Its lead image was a girl placing a candle at a fountain in Tel Aviv’s Dizengoff Square, where photos of victims of the attack on Israel sat alongside photos of Israeli soldiers killed while committing genocide in Gaza. The pages featured dozens of images of Israeli commemorations; of people weeping, embracing and bowing their heads in remembrance, as they should, because they deserve to heal and to remember their loved ones like anyone else. The point, though, is that with the genocide ongoing, there were only a handful of Palestinians briefly featured, all of them currently living through hell - and not a single blog post was reserved for the Palestinians killed by Israel on 7 October 2023 itself. The entries on Gaza were so fleeting and by-the-numbers that all they did was underline the disparity. They reeked of afterthought, or of an attempt to see off criticism. There was no space for the seven Dos children, who were wiped from mainstream media memory as 7 October victims because they were Palestinian. Taboo subject The Guardian’s live blog , headlined “World leaders pay tribute to victims as Israel marks three years since 7 October attack by Hamas - as it happened”, was more of the same. Palestinians were featured, but as footnotes drowned out by Israel’s mourning. In the US , NBC’s live updates , which focused on how Israel was marking the anniversary with memorials “at homes, roadsides, kibbutzim and a music festival site”, gave more room than others to Palestinians - but in doing so, exposed another dichotomy. It communicated, or at least implied, to the reader that the Israelis killed three years ago were more important than the Palestinians it rightly pointed out were still being killed. Even on the anniversary itself, at least five Palestinians were killed , including a 17-year-old boy and a rescue worker responding to a previous strike. The fact is, talking about the Palestinians killed on 7 October is a taboo - one fiercely policed by pro-Israel lobbying groups and the western media and political classes. The opening line of a BBC report on an anniversary march in London to demand an end to the genocide said that organisers were “ignoring a request by the Metropolitan Police” for it to be called off. Police, it continued, were worried that the march, organised by the University of London coalition, would distress Jewish students and staff. It then quoted the Union of Jewish Students as saying that the protest was “provocative, deliberate and must be condemned”. The BBC only briefly - without naming or, it appears, interviewing anyone - mentioned that protest organisers said they wanted to denounce genocide and fight for a free Palestine. Over on the Guardian , a statement from the Board of Deputies of British Jews was published in full, calling the protesters, some of whom were Jewish, a “small and extremist minority of British society”. The UK ’s defence secretary, Wes Streeting, was featured labelling the march “shameful”. Not a single marcher was quoted. Media manipulation The strength of the taboo was also demonstrated by the hysterical reactions from the pro-Israel lobby, along with right-wing and centrist politicians, to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s statement on the day, to which the media hungrily responded. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); News stories in the US were not framed around what Mamdani actually said. Instead, they centred on the absurd response to it. It’s worth noting that his statement began not with Gaza, but with a condemnation of the Hamas-led attacks, which he called “horrific war crimes” that were “profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers”. But that wasn’t enough. Mamdani’s transgression, it seems, was that he went on to condemn the genocide, pointing out how many people were killed and underscoring the fact that despite the “so-called ceasefire”, the slaughter continues. Israel's genocide against the Palestinian people began on 7 October 2023. It continues. And Palestinian lives are as important as Israeli lives The New York Times, CNN and Politico all centred their stories around the three paragraphs in which the mayor focused on Palestinians. Mamdani “draws anger”, the New York Times headline said . For CNN , he drew “ire”. And in the telling of Politico’s headline , he was subject to “bipartisan backlash”. Those three stories, from some of the most esteemed outlets in the US, collectively provide a pitch-perfect example of media manipulation in action at the highest levels. Here are the facts: Israel’s genocide against the Palestinian people began on 7 October 2023. It continues. And Palestinian lives are as important as Israeli lives. That’s the simple truth, whether the western media wants to tell it or not. What does the UAE own in the UK? Football clubs, London landmarks and billion-pound assets Submitted by Daniel Tester on Mon, 10/19/2026 - 14:44 Abu Dhabi and Dubai's vast investments are facing scrutiny amid allegations against Manchester City Football Club and pressure on PM Andy Burnham UAE investments in the UK include, from left, DP World, owner of P&O Ferries; parts of Berkeley Square in Mayfair, London; and Manchester City Football Club (all AFP). On The UAE is one of the world’s richest countries, with its seven monarchies owning sovereign wealth funds worth in excess of $2 trillion. Fuelled by revenues from oil as well as finance, tourism and the gold trade, it has invested billions internationally, holding vast stakes in everything from banks to airports and restaurant chains across North America, Europe and beyond. But this partnership is facing unprecedented scrutiny in the UK, where the UAE has committed to invest almost $30bn for the period 2021-2026 through the UAE–UK Sovereign Investment Partnership. In September, Manchester City Football Club, owned by Emirati royal and vice-president Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nayhan, was found to have breached 114 Premier League financial rules by disguising more than £830m ($1.1bn) in illicit funding. The club denies the claims. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is at the heart of the storm, having served as Manchester mayor from 2017 until June, during which time Emirati cash transformed both Manchester City football club and the wider city . Doing business with the UAE has only become more controversial given its role in Sudan ’s civil war , where it is accused of supporting the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group whose mass killings UN investigators say bear the “ hallmarks of genocide ”. The UAE denies the allegations. But Burnham is also keen to balance public uproar against the UAE with the steady flow of Gulf investment, which both defenders of the football club and the government say has boosted economic growth. If nothing else, the rows have exposed just how many UK institutions Abu Dhabi and Dubai, the wealthiest emirates and biggest investors, have a stake in. Sport Manchester City was bought by Abu Dhabi United Group, a private equity firm owned by the Emirati royal Mansour bin Zayed, in 2008 for £200m. At the time, Manchester City was not an elite club, usually finishing mid-table and getting relegated in 2001. But since the sale, the club has dominated top-flight English football, winning eight Premier League titles, plus the Uefa Champions League. Khaldoon al-Mubarak , an adviser to Abu Dhabi’s royal family and CEO of its Mubadala sovereign wealth fund, is the club’s chairman, while the club’s stadium is named the Etihad Arena, after Abu Dhabi’s government-owned airline. Emirates sponsors both Arsenal (left) and the FA Cup (both AFP); the UAE-owned Godolphin stable has produced winners, including Sakhee, here ridden by Frankie Dettori in 2001 (Reuters) The UAE also has stakes elsewhere in the Premier League. In 2004, the airline Emirates, owned by the government of Dubai, purchased naming rights to Arsenal’s home ground, now called the Emirates Stadium, and the club’s shirt sponsorship for £100m . The deal was renewed in August until 2033 for an undisclosed fee. The airline has also sponsored the FA Cup since 2015, and Lancashire Cricket Club since 2013. Abu Dhabi’s CYVN Holdings has a minority stake in McLaren Racing, which owns McLaren’s Formula One team, based in Woking, southern England and was the winner of back-to-back Teams’ Championships in 2025. Bahrain’s Mumtalakat fund owns the rest of the stake, as well as parent company McLaren Group . CYVN separately bought McLaren’s car manufacturing business, McLaren Automotive, outright in 2025 for an undisclosed fee. Dubai’s royal family owns Godolphin, the world’s largest horseracing team that operates the biggest stable in the UK outside Newmarket in Suffolk, eastern England. Through Godolphin and other horses, Dubai royals have won the British Flat Racing Champion Owner title 31 times since 1985, including this year. Property Besides owning Manchester City football club, the UAE also owns lucrative property developments across the city. Among the largest is Manchester Life , a glitzy, mixed-use regeneration project in Manchester’s Ancoats area launched in 2014 in a deal between Manchester City Council and the Abu Dhabi United Group reportedly worth £1bn. Abu Dhabi also invested an undisclosed figure in Manchester’s Co-Op Live arena, through its 81 percent share of the City Football Group, which in turn owns 47.5 percent of the UK's largest indoor venue. Berkeley Square in Mayfair is among the London properties owned by the UAE (AFP) It emerged in October that Manchester City Council gave Sheikh Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group the right of first refusal on some of these projects in what critics have dubbed a “sweetheart deal” that sidelined rival developers. In London, the Emirati royal family amassed a property empire under Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed bin Sultan al-Nahyan, ruler of the UAE from 2004 until his death in 2022. Valued in 2020 at over £5bn, this includes luxury properties in some of London’s most expensive areas, including Mayfair and Knightsbridge, much of which was acquired via opaque companies registered in tax havens. Abu Dhabi also picked up country estates in the Scottish Highlands and Surrey, and owns London’s Excel exhibition centre, the city’s largest conference hall. Much of this property has since been divided up among Khalifa’s heirs, although which Emirati royal owns what isn’t always clear. Since then, the UAE’s property spree has continued. In 2023, a real estate firm owned by Abu Dhabi’s government bought London Square , the developer behind London’s controversial Nine Elms regeneration project, for $291m. It announced earlier this month plans to build a further 9,000 homes at the site. Ports, shipping and infrastructure DP World, the Dubai government’s ports and logistics giant, owns London Gateway and Southampton, the UK’s second and third largest shipping terminals by container volume. The London site was approved for a £1bn expansion by the government in 2024. Part of the UK’s freeports scheme , the ports are special economic zones in which DP World and other businesses pay less tax and face weaker regulation than they would elsewhere in the UK. DP World also owns P&O, the UK’s long-established shipping company, sold off from public ownership in 2006 for £3.6bn. It separately bought P&O Ferries in 2019 for £322m. DP World, owned by Dubai, bought UK ferry operator P&O Ferries in 2019 (AFP) In 2022, DP World faced heavy criticism, including from the UK government , for sacking 800 of P&O Ferries’ British staff and replacing them with foreign agency workers paid less than the UK minimum wage. But DP World consolidated its logistics empire further in August when it purchased six grocery distribution centres serving Asda, Sainsbury’s and the Co-op from the US conglomerate GXO Logistics. The UAE has also targeted tech. Abu Dhabi's Mubadala invested an undisclosed sum into Yondr in 2024, one of the operators of a data centre campus in Slough on the outskirts of London. And Masdar, the UAE’s state-owned renewable energy company, has stakes in the UK’s wind farms, including the London Array off the coast of Kent and Dogger Bank South in the North Sea. Mubadala meanwhile holds a minority stake in CityFibre, the UK’s third largest network provider, as of 2021. In 2011 Abu Dhabi bought a 9.9 percent stake in Thames Water, although the UAE wrote off the investment as worthless in its 2024 accounts, amid the utility firm’s financial toils. Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth fund also owns nearly eight percent of London Gatwick, the UK’s second busiest airport, having sold down its stake from 15 percent in 2018. It has coveted owning part of Heathrow. Abu Dhabi was also approached as a potential investor into the Sizewell C nuclear power plant in 2023 , before the shares were instead sold to the French state-owned energy firm EDF and a Canadian pension fund, among other investors. In July, Etisalat, a telecoms firm majority-owned by the UAE government, sold its £4.4bn stake in Vodafone, the British telecoms multinational, after its ownership was called a “national security risk” by the UK government and it was forced to establish a special committee overseeing sensitive work. Finance and research In 2024, Abu Dhabi gained a one-third stake in Hargreaves Lansdown, the UK’s largest retail investment house, in a £5.4bn takeover alongside American and European private equity firms. Later that year, Mubadala bought an undisclosed stake in the British digital bank Revolut as part of a $500m secondary share sale. The Barclays HQ in Canary Wharf: the UAE invested in the bank after the financial crash of 2008 (AFP) Sheikh Mansour attracted controversy in 2008 when he and investors from Qatar bought a 16 percent share in Barclays during the global financial crisis. Worth an estimated £4bn, the deal helped the bank avoid a government bailout imposed on some of its rivals, to which conditions were attached. The Financial Conduct Authority in 2024 fined Barclays £40m for misleading its shareholders about payments of over £300m to Qatari investors involved in the deal. Abu Dhabi sold all of its stakes by 2013. The UK is also courting Emirati investment for a “growth corridor” located between Oxford and Cambridge that the government has dubbed "the UK’s Silicon Valley”. But the UAE is now reportedly threatening to pull out of the plans amid fallout over its guilty verdict in the Manchester City case. Hospitality and retail The UAE has stakes on British high streets, much of which it acquired in 2024 when Mubadala bought a 68 percent share of equity owned by Fortress Investment Group, a US firm with over $55bn of assets under management. Customers wait outside The Ivy restaurant in the city centre of Manchester in October 2020 (AFP) In the UK, Fortress owns Punch Pubs, which operates 1,400 pubs and bars across the country, the cinema chain Curzon, the budget shop Poundstretcher, and the wine retailer Majestic. In April, Sheikh Tahnoon's International Holding Company paid £1.4bn for the restaurant empire of hospitality mogul Richard Caring, which includes the Ivy chain and the elite member’s club Annabel’s in Mayfair’s Berkeley Square, where the UAE also owns other properties. Media Abu Dhabi launched a bid to buy the Telegraph newspaper and Spectator magazine in 2023 alongside the US private equity firm Redbird Capital Partners. The deal, which was headed by Sheikh Mansour, sparked massive scrutiny over censorship concerns, and ultimately fell through after the UK government introduced new laws barring leaders of foreign governments from owning media companies. The Telegraph was instead sold to the German media giant Axel Springer in June, while the Spectator was bought by GB News co-owner Paul Marshall in September 2024. But Abu Dhabi has gained a stake in media elsewhere via its takeover of Fortress, which led a lender consortium that bought Vice Media Group in 2023 after the broadcaster and magazine filed for bankruptcy. Vice had months earlier signed a lucrative partnership with the MBC Group, a media company backed by the UAE’s sometime rival, Saudi Arabia . Analysis: UK Muslims face highest rate of hate crimes but police figures undercount them Submitted by Imran Mulla on Thu, 10/22/2026 - 09:58 Data indicates Muslims in Britain are the most likely group to face both religious and race-based hate crime Britain's Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood pictured in the House of Commons on 13 July (AFP) Off Are hate crimes against Muslims in Britain being under-counted and even downplayed? “Jewish people are almost 10 times more likely than Muslims to be victims of religious hate crimes,” The Times newspaper reported on 30 April. “Per head of population Jews experienced more than eight times as many hate crime incidents as Muslims,” according to BBC Panorama that same month. In July 2026 Lord John Mann, the government’s antisemitism tsar, said that “Jewish people proportionately face the highest level of reported hate crime of any religious group”. While the surge in antisemitism has been recognised in mainstream political discourse, at the same time hate crimes targeting Muslims appear to have been significantly underrepresented in police data. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); A recently published Home Office report indicates that Muslims face the highest rate of hate crimes in the country, but this is not being reflected in police data. Labour MP John McDonnell told Middle East Eye: “This serious under-estimation of the hate crimes against Muslims by the police and other authorities skews the policies needed in place to protect the Muslim community.” Labour minister: British Muslims haven't always been heard but Burnham will change that Read More » He added: “Unless this is acknowledged and addressed it could put Muslims at further risk. I am urging the government to urgently recognise the seriousness of this issue.” When hate crimes are presented in the media or discussed by senior politicians, including members of the government, police figures tend to be referenced. According to the police record of religious hate crimes in 2025, 12 out of every 10,000 Muslims faced a hate crime in the "religion" category, while 106 out of 10,000 Jews did so. There are multiple categories of hate crime, including "religion" and "race". The police data does not record the religion of victims of hate crimes in the "race" category, which makes it significantly less comprehensive than data published every three years by the Crime Survey of England and Wales (CSEW). According to CSEW data for April 2022 to March 2025, 1 percent of Muslims experienced a hate crime in the “race” category and 0.8 percent experienced one in the “religion” category. This data showed that Muslims were the most likely group to face both religious and race-based hate crime of any religious and ethnic group. In comparison, the figures for Asian people were 0.7 percent for race and 0.5 percent for religion; for Black people 0.7 percent for race and 0.1 percent for religion; for Sikhs 0.5 percent for race and 0.1 percent for religion; for Jewish people 0.2 percent for race and 0.4 percent for religion. Discrepancy in hate crime figures The Office for Statistics Regulation has advised that police and CSEW statistics should be “used alongside each other” in order to provide a more “complete picture of hate crime”. This is rarely done in citations and coverage. The Home Office report on police-recorded hate crimes covering the year up to March 2026, which was published earlier this month, shows that 13 out of 10,000 Muslims have suffered a hate crime. But the report notes that CSEW figures, “published in 2025, estimated that 0.8% of Muslims experienced a religious hate crime per year on average, compared with 0.4% of Jewish people.” What explains the significant gulf between police and CSEW figures? UK settlements ban: How conspiracy theory accusing Burnham of courting 'Islamist voters' went global Read More » The Home Office report said: “The different pattern between the two data sources may be due to the likelihood of a crime being reported to the police and the different coverage between the sources.” A January 2026 survey by the parliamentary Women and Equalities Committee indicated that as few 12.5 percent of Muslim females reported hate crimes they experienced, which suggests most anti-Muslim hate crimes are not counted. The Jewish Voice for Liberation group (JVL), which has met the Office for Statistics Regulation on the matter, said in an analysis of the data: “Police recorded hate crime data has recognised limitations. They are exposed to a significant variation in victim reporting rates and police recording procedures, and they do not publish victim religion under the much larger strand of Race. “CSEW data relates to a direct victim survey and is therefore neither affected by variable victim reporting rates, nor by differences in police recording.” JVL added: “The Home Office’s advice always to present CSEW data alongside police statistics for a more reliable assessment has largely been ignored by the media, politicians and, worryingly, even governments.” 'This is a shared experience' Jenny Manson, a co-chair of JVL, told MEE: “We had a very useful meeting with the Office for Statistics Regulation.” (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); She added that “they told us they would report our findings to the Home Office” and advise it to qualify its hate crimes report for the year ending March 2026. Manson noted that the recently released report gave “greater prominence” to the CSEW statistics. “Some attempts are made to explain this difference [with the police figures] but this does not go deep enough. “Muslims and Jews are facing an undoubted increase in Islamophobia and in antisemitism,” Manson said. “We know that the best way to counter this is to recognise that such prejudice and religious and racial hatred are interlinked; this is a shared experience. “The double standards shown towards Muslims, particularly from the right, by minimising Islamophobia, are very destructive to both our communities.” Dr Alan Maddison, who conducted the analysis published by the JVL, told MEE the Home Office should record the religion and ethnicity of victims in both the “race” and “religion” categories. “Until then they should publish all victim group CSEW data every year in their annual reports, and address the contradiction with police-recorded religious hate crime rates,” Maddison added. Can Iran negotiate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis? Submitted by Zahra Ladha on Thu, 10/22/2026 - 09:54 Tehran launches a diplomatic initiative in an attempt to bring both sides to the negotiating table Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighters ride on the back of a truck during battles against Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis at the Jabal Han front west of the city of Taiz on 21 October 2026 (AFP) Off As the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis continued to escalate, Iran , a longstanding ally of the Yemeni group, offered to mediate between the two sides on 11 October. Eleven days later, neither side has accepted Iran’s offer. There is little indication that either the Houthis or Saudi Arabia are prepared to return to the negotiating table in the near term. Yahya Saree, a spokesperson for the Houthis - officially named Ansar Allah - reaffirmed on Monday that attacks on Saudi Arabia will continue until Riyadh ends the “financial and economic siege on the Yemeni people”, which the group says has been imposed on Yemeni ports of entry for nearly 12 years. Saree also said the attacks would continue until Saudi Arabia halted its military operations against the group. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Analysts believe Riyadh is probably unwilling to meet these demands. "I do not foresee the Saudi-led coalition or Yemen’s internationally recognised government conceding to Houthi demands for full control over Yemen’s airspace and maritime access, along with billions of dollars of compensation," Mohammed Basha, an expert on Yemeni affairs, told Middle East Eye. "Such concessions would effectively reward the Houthis militarily, politically and financially without securing meaningful guarantees for lasting peace." In the meantime, the Houthis are likely to continue escalating attacks, while Saudi Arabia leverages its regional and international partnerships to defend its territory. Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces has intensified across several fronts, including in Taiz and Marib, further complicating the prospects for a durable settlement. Even if Saudi Arabia and the Houthis find enough common ground to begin negotiations, which appears unlikely, the most likely outcome is a fragile ceasefire. "Beyond the restrictions on airports and ports and economic compensation, the Houthis’ demands include access to oil and gas revenues, and importantly, political recognition," Alex Jalili told MEE. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); "I would therefore distinguish between a temporary cessation of attacks, which could certainly emerge from negotiations, and a more durable settlement." Diverging interests According to a statement by Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Aragchi on Tuesday, both the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have yet to respond to Tehran’s offer of mediation. For Riyadh, the decision to accept Iranian mediation would carry implications beyond the immediate conflict with the Houthis. Demonstrating deterrence against the Houthis and other Tehran-linked groups has been a key priority for Riyadh amid the US-Israeli war on Iran. This was particularly evident when Saudi Arabia and the US launched joint air strikes on Iraq on 29 July, targeting Iran-linked groups there. At the same time, as the ongoing conflict reshapes the regional balance of power, Riyadh is also attempting to demonstrate its position in the emerging security order, including through the signing of the Mecca Pact with Turkey and Pakistan. 'Iran wants to preserve the leverage that the Houthis provide without allowing that leverage to produce an uncontrollable escalation' - Sina Toossi, analyst Accepting Tehran’s mediation in a conflict with the Houthis, which Riyadh characterises as an Iranian proxy, would probably undermine both objectives. Beyond this, Houthi-Saudi Arabia negotiations can be managed by other regional interlocutors. “Riyadh already has established channels of communication with the Houthis including through Oman. Accepting Tehran as mediator could also reinforce the perception that Iran is the ultimate guarantor of Houthi behaviour, something Riyadh has little interest in legitimising,” Jalili told MEE. Still, Riyadh’s reluctance to accept Iranian mediation over the Houthi conflict should not be conflated with an unwillingness to engage with Tehran more broadly. Last Thursday Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy confirmed that Riyadh maintains direct communication with Tehran. The Houthis also appear to assess that further attacks on Saudi Arabia will increase their leverage in later negotiations. “The Houthis have demonstrated that they can threaten critical infrastructure, disrupt economic activity and exploit vulnerabilities in Saudi air defences. That gives them considerable leverage, which they are unlikely to relinquish in exchange for marginal concessions,” Jalili added. As a result, the Houthis are unlikely to accept Iranian mediation until they believe they have made sufficient military gains to strengthen their position in negotiations. Iran’s objectives Mediating the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis would probably allow Iran to shape the terms of a ceasefire while leaving the door open to renewed conflict. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); "Iran would likely favour a comprehensive agreement that builds on the 2022 ceasefire, including arrangements over Yemen’s ports, airports, salaries and reconstruction, alongside credible Saudi security guarantees," Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Centre for International Policy, told MEE. Yet a comprehensive agreement would not necessarily produce a durable settlement. A fragile truce that preserves the Houthis’ ability to resume hostilities could ultimately better serve Tehran’s strategic interests amid the US-Israeli war on Iran. The renewed hostilities have also provided Tehran with another means of pressuring Riyadh. On 20 July, the Houthis announced a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia in response to Saudi air strikes on Sanaa International Airport and what they describe as a wider blockade of Yemen's airports and ports. Gulf exports more oil than it did before Iran war despite surge in Hormuz attacks Read More » With Iranian threats to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz compounded by Houthi threats around Bab el-Mandeb, Tehran has additional means of exerting pressure on regional energy exports. Tehran, like Riyadh and other regional capitals, is also attempting to shape the emerging post-war order in the region. A stronger Houthi position in Yemen could also help preserve Tehran's regional influence as the war reshapes the balance of power. At the same time, Iran needs to ensure that the road to a ceasefire does not prompt a wider regional conflagration. “There is a fundamental tension here: Iran wants to preserve the leverage that the Houthis provide without allowing that leverage to produce an uncontrollable escalation,” Toossi told MEE. Such an escalation would probably further undermine Tehran’s already fractious relationship with Saudi Arabia. Indeed, Riyadh has already accused Tehran of encouraging the Houthi escalation in violation of its commitments under the 2023 rapprochement agreement. While unlikely on current indications, an uncontrolled escalation might include offensive campaigns by Turkey or Pakistan, signatories of the Mecca Pact, against the Houthis, or a UK entry into the conflict beyond defensive support for Saudi Arabia. Such a scenario could see Iran-linked groups in Iraq, which have had close cooperation with the Houthis for several years, drawn into the conflict. And the failure to contain such a regionalisation of the conflict could plausibly push some Gulf states to take a more aggressive stance against Tehran, undermining prospects for any renewed negotiations between Iran and the US. For Tehran, the challenge will therefore be to preserve the strategic leverage afforded by the Houthis without allowing the conflict to undermine its wider regional and diplomatic interests. Suspect should not be deprived of bail in case of 'reasonable doubt' over involvement, SC rules. ISLAMABAD: Taking exception to the prosecution’s shifting stance without realising the gravity of that conduct in a case regarding expired drugs, the Supreme Court has ruled that whenever reasonable doubt arises, a suspect should not be deprived of the benefit of bail. The object of a trial is to make an under-trial suspect answer criminal trial instead of punishing by letting him rot behind bars, regretted Justice Muhammad Ali Mazhar in a verdict published on Wednesday. He was heading a three-member bench that on July 22 heard a criminal appeal filed by Muhammad Akbar, who was originally granted bail by the SC on April 16 in a case registered at Quetta’s New Sariab Police Station. The SC extended the bail granted earlier on the same terms and conditions, adding that observations made in this bail order were tentative in nature and will not prejudice the case pending before the trial court of either party. “We are of the firm view that the case of the petitioner requires further inquiry,” Justice Mazhar said in a five-page order. “Whenever reasonable doubt arises with regard to the participation of the accused in the crime or the truth or probability of the prosecution case as well as the evidence proposed to be produced in support of the charge, the accused should not be deprived of benefit of bail and in such a situation it would be better to keep him on bail than in jail during the trial,” the order read. Justice Mazhar narrated the sequence of events, noting that the original case was lodged against the suspect under Sections 379, 420, 274, 275, and 276 of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), as well as Sections 23 and 27 of the Drugs Act 1976 , concerning transportation of expired drugs. These sections deal with offences affecting public health and safety since they relate to drug adulteration and misrepresentation, and carry penalties up to six months of imprisonment. Based on these sections, a two-judge SC bench on April 16 granted post-arrest bail to the petitioner on furnishing bail bonds to the tune of Rs100,000 with two sureties in the like amount to the satisfaction of the trial court. When the SC’s bail order was sent for compliance, it emerged that the prosecution modified the first information report (FIR) by replacing the original provisions with Sections 409, 471, 468, 467, 420, 109 of PPC, read with Section 5 (2) of the 1947 Prevention of Corruption Act . These sections outline major white-collar and financial crimes involving public servants, forgery, cheating, and abetment. Frequently combined in corruption, bank fraud and property misappropriation-related cases, the provisions spell out severe punishments, ranging from 10 years in jail to life imprisonment. During the July hearing, when the court confronted state counsel Baqir Shah and Investigating Officer (IO) Muhammad Ajmal about why the FIR was modified by adding new sections of the PPC, they responded that these additions were made on Jan 15 but failed to offer any plausible reason why the modified FIR was not brought on record when the SC granted bail. They could also not justify deletion of Section 23 and 27 of the Drugs Act 1976 from the FIR when the initial allegation against the petitioner was transporting the expired drugs with alleged violations of the Drugs Act. When the court asked the IO what new evidence was brought on record which necessitated these insertions, he simply replied that four statements of witnesses were recorded under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC). He further said the prosecuting Quetta deputy superintendent of police sought the opinion of the deputy inspector general (Legal), who opined to delete and add new sections. “It appears from the conduct of the prosecution that to complicate the case with some ulterior motives, the prosecution acted unfairly and added certain sections without realising the effect of deleting these sections of the Drugs Act,” Justice Mazhar observed. He said another aim may be to frustrate and deprive the petitioner of concession of bail. Though Justice Mazhar refrained from adverse observations since the matter was still pending with the trial court, he regretted that, due to the concealment of facts, the possibility cannot be ruled out that new sections were added after court order only to deprive the petitioner of bail. “We are sanguine that new section/offence can be inserted, provided that something was gleaned to the prosecution on investigation of crime but not on the whims of prosecution,” Justice Mazhar stated. He remarked that the prosecution has “not acted seriously” and that if any insertion was made before the bail was granted, it should have been brought to the SC’s knowledge “for consideration without playing hide and seek”. The judge regretted that due to “such callous conduct”, the petitioner who was earlier granted bail was still behind the bars. Due to divergent pleas of the prosecution, as well as insertion and deletion of new and old sections of PPC in the same FIR during trial, the case has otherwise been made out to be a case of further inquiry, the judgment said. “The prosecution is itself confused regarding the culpability of the petitioner due to changing stances,” it observed, adding the case of further inquiry presupposes tentative assessment which may create doubt with respect to the involvement of the suspect in the crime.

Execute scripts sequentially function runNextScript(idx) { if (idx >= executableScripts.length) { // Free inert and payloads after initialization var cleanup = shadow.querySelectorAll('template, script[type="text/plain"]'); for (var c = 0; c The government on Wednesday decreased the price of petrol by Rs2.71 per litre, but raised that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Re0.31. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs379.31 per litre while HSD will cost Rs390.11 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 22 (Thursday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

‘Journalist safety laws only on paper due to weak complaint systems’. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan’s laws ai­­m­­ed at protecting journalists from threats and attacks risk remaining largely “on paper” unless the federal and provincial safety commissions are given more powers, accessible complaint mechanisms and the resources needed to deliver timely protection, says a new report released by Freedom Network, a media watchdog, on Wednesday. The report, titled “From safety on paper to safety in practice”, is an as­­s­essment of the work carried out by two commissions — one appointed by the federal government and the other by the Sindh government. The Islamabad-based Freedom Network produced the research with assistance from the International Media Support (IMS). Authored by Minahil Shahab and Adnan Rehmat, the report examined the commissions’ capacity and operational constraints through consultations with stakeholders, interviews and a baseline online survey of around 40 working journalists in Sindh, including respondents from the province’s rural areas. According to report, 65pc of respondents say they have faced work-related threats or interference According to the report, parliament enacted two special laws to combat impunity for crimes against journalists and the media in 2022. Both the federal and Sindh governments instituted commissions to enforce the laws. The online survey found 70 per cent of the respondents knew a provincial protection law existed, but 65pc of them did not know where to find the commission’s office, obtain information, website or complaint route. Sixty-five per cent of the respondents reported experiencing work-related threats or interference since 2021. These findings describe the surveyed group rather than establishing province-wide prevalence. Challenges pinpointed The assessment identified distinct institutional challenges. Kamal Ud­­d­in Tipu, the federal commission’s cha­­irperson, spoke of staffing, budget, and administrative constraints during the research. With the federal commission now operational, the priority is to ensure that its personnel, resources and complaint systems support timely protection and sustained follow-up. In Sindh, the report documented an established institution with premises, meetings, complaints and engagement with police and media organisations. However, union representatives and non-official members described delayed responses, limited outreach beyond Karachi and dependence on police replies. The Sindh commission’s chairperson, Aijaz Ahmed Memon, disputed suggestions that journalists lacked trust in the institution and reported improvements in coordination, case activity and outreach plans. The report also highlighted media employers’ responsibilities. Fifty-one per cent of the respondents said employers had not informed them about safety procedures, emergency contacts, insurance, legal assistance or complaint mechanisms. The Sindh chairperson separately reported that 44 media outlets had not replied to the commission’s queries. Recommendations include confidential and accessible complaint routes, urgent risk assessment, designated caseworkers, police escalation procedures, stronger employer cooperation and publication of anonymised outcomes and spending. The report said amendments nee­ded to be framed carefully in order to address documented legal barriers. The Freedom Network called for coordinated action by governments, commissions, police, media employers and journalist organisations to deliver positive results and ensure that journalists can obtain effective assistance when threats arise. Draft auto policy revs up hopes for cheaper vehicles. • PHEVs may see price reductions of over 20pc under proposed tax changes • Petrol, hybrid vehicles may become around 8-10pc cheaper • Parts makers warn rising CBU imports, lower tariffs to hurt local industry KARACHI: The draft Auto Policy 2026-31 could trigger one of the biggest shake-ups in the country’s automobile market, with prices of some vehicles potentially falling by more than 20 per cent. However, the prospect of cheaper cars may create an unusual predicament, as buyers are likely to hold back purchases in anticipation of lower prices, causing anxiety among automakers over the value of their existing inventory. According to Topline Securities, the new draft maintains the 1pc general sales tax (GST) rate on battery electric vehicles (BEVs), while setting rates at 9pc for plug-in hybrid vehicles (PHEVs) and 6pc for range-extended electric vehicles (REEVs). The earlier draft had proposed a uniform 1pc GST across all new energy vehicles (NEVs), while the previous policy imposed rates of 8.5pc to 12.75pc on PHEVs. This points to the government’s priority to incentivise the rollout of NEVs, particularly BEVs. Preliminary industry estimates suggest conventional petrol vehicles could become approximately 8-10pc cheaper, while hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) may see reductions of around 9pc. PHEVs could benefit even more, with estimated price reductions exceeding 20pc. Among BEVs, models with import values below $15,000 could see reductions of approximately 22pc compared to around 8pc for higher-priced BEVs. However, REEVs may become around 3pc more expensive under the proposed tax structure. The new draft proposes reducing tariffs on localised completely knocked-down (CKD) parts to 15pc by FY31 from 25pc previously. Topline Securities said the reduction could be detrimental to the local vendor industry, adding that the benefits were likely to be passed on to consumers amid intense competition. Parts makers sound alarm Pakistan Association of Automotive Parts and Accessories Manufacturers (PAPAAM) Chairman Abdur Rehman Aizaz said the new auto policy amounted to a “conspiracy to destroy several industries”. He said rising imports of new and used cars were already hurting the developed local auto parts industry, which now faced the threat of closures because of government policies. Mr Aizaz pointed out that imports of completely built-up (CBU) new cars rose to 2,407 units in September from 391 in August, while imports of used cars increased to 2,454 units from 1,185 over the same period. He said every new or used imported vehicle reduced potential volumes for the country’s 1,200 local auto parts manufacturers. Locally produced parts accounted for approximately Rs1.5 million of the value of each domestically assembled vehicle, he added. On that basis, the 4,861 CBU vehicles imported in September represented an estimated Rs7.3 billion in lost revenue for local parts manufacturers, Mr Aizaz said. Industry representatives said the GAC Aion UT, currently priced at around Rs6.4m, could fall to Rs5m-Rs5.2m. Higher-priced electric SUVs such as the BYD Atto 3 and GAC Aion V, priced at around Rs9m, could also see meaningful reductions. They said popular petrol and hybrid models could become more affordable as well. Industry estimates indicate potential savings of around Rs600,000 to Rs800,000 on selected variants of the Honda HR-V e:HEV, Haval Jolion and Toyota Corolla Altis. The biggest absolute reductions could emerge in the PHEV segment. A Jaecoo J7 PHEV, priced near Rs10m, could potentially fall to around Rs8m, while the Kia Sorento PHEV, which has already witnessed substantial price adjustments, could face further downward pressure from changes in GST and import duties. Sania Irfan of Topline Securities said the new draft proposed a zero per cent automotive development levy (ADL) on fossil fuel-driven vehicles below 1,000cc, 2pc on 1,000-2,000cc vehicles and 10pc on those above 2,000cc, replacing the earlier draft’s rates of 4.5-5.5pc across engine categories. Kalbe Ali in Islamabad also contributed to this report Published in Dawn, October 22nd, 2026

Pakistan, Qatar, Turkiye and Indonesia sign 'Badr' defence cooperation pact. Pakistan, Qatar, Turkiye and Indonesia on Wednesday signed a multilateral pact to promote cooperation in defence production and capabilities, the Turkish defence ministry said. The signing took place in Qatar, with ministers of the four countries attending the ceremony. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif represented Pakistan at the signing. The Foreign Office has yet to comment on the signing of the defence pact, but Asif posted on X his “key statements” on the ‘Badr Memorandum of Understanding’ (MoU). The remarks were posted as a visual share, which said: “Pakistan places great importance on strengthening defence cooperation with trusted partners. This memorandum reflects Islamabad’s shared commitment to contributing to regional peace and stability. “We look forward to exploring opportunities for strengthening self-reliance, industrial collaboration, joint production and technology transfer while drawing on the complementary strengths of our respective defence industries, in accordance with relevant international and domestic laws and regulations.” The statement further said, “Through this partnership, we aim to advance cooperation across joint research and development, training exchanges and industrial capability building.” Turkiye and Qatar released similar statements on the signing of the pact. Reuters quoted the Turkish ministry as saying that the pact, titled ‘Badr Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)’, was aimed at defence cooperation and strengthening defensive capabilities. “The agreement holds substantial economic importance,” it said, adding the accord sought to foster cooperation in military production, boost military capabilities, and help collaboration in technical military training, research and development. “By leveraging the unique military production capabilities of each country, the initiative will facilitate cooperation and integration, enhance defence industrial capacities, and enable the fulfilment of the needs of allied and friendly nations,” it added. Later, the Qatari defence ministry also released a similar statement. Turkish Defence Minister Yaşar Güler, Qatar’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of State for Defence Sheikh Saud bin Abdulrahman, and Indonesia’s Deputy Minister of Defence Yusuf Jauhari were the other signatories. Haluk Görgün, who heads Turkiye’s Secretariat of Defence Industries , was also present on the occasion. Görgün said in a statement that the accord formed the foundation of a “strategic cooperation” to develop joint production and technology. “Technology sharing, joint development and strengthening domestic production capabilities lie at the heart of sustainable defence industry. As Turkiye, we value partnerships that go beyond off-the-shelf procurement models, that foster the development of a nation’s own human capital and industrial infrastructure,” Gorgun said. “We believe that the Badr MoU will contribute to transforming the complementary capabilities of Qatar, Pakistan, Indonesia, and Turkiye into concrete projects,” he added. State-run Qatar News Agency said the pact was named ‘Badr’, “referring to the full moon, to signify how the four nations complement one another through this agreement, given its immense importance in terms of both defence and the economy”. “Other friendly nations may join the MoU, in accordance with criteria agreed upon by the four countries,” it said. Pakistan has strong brotherly and historic ties with the three countries, with intense diplomatic engagement seen in recent months with Qatar and Turkiye particularly. Pakistan and Turkiye, along with Saudi Arabia, are members of the Makkah Defence Alliance , under which they are to treat an attack against any of them as an attack against all. Qatar had welcomed that pact as cooperation aimed at regional security and stability. Islamabad and Doha have remained engaged as mediators in the US-Iran war. Meanwhile, Pakistan and Turkiye are part of the Regional Four (R4) Group along with Saudi Arabia and Egypt, which emerged in March and has met several times since then. Earlier this week, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi met his Qatari counterpart during his visit to Doha, where the two agreed to boost bilateral cooperation in internal security. During his November 2025 visit to the Gulf state, President Asif Ali Zardari met with Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and offered to expand bilateral cooperation in the areas of defence production. Last month, Indonesian naval chief Admiral Dr Muhammad Ali called on Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir in Rawalpindi. The two sides “reaffirmed their resolve to further strengthen cooperation, particularly in the domains of professional training, defence collaboration and joint exercises”, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said. The naval chief had also met President Asif Ali Zardari. In January, Defence Minister retired Lieutenant General Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin had called on CDF Munir, with ISPR saying he expressed Jakarta’s desire to further expand defence ties with Pakistan.

PTI leadership ‘turns on itself’ after protest debacle. Salman Akram Raja • Raja ‘rebukes’ move by KP lawmakers to nominate Gandapur as interim KP president • Ex-CM fires back, demands apology from secy gen over ‘name-calling’ PESHAWAR: The debacle that befell the PTI’s recent protest march has led to serious fissures within the core committee, with demands emerging from within for chan­ges at the leadership level that can steer the party out of its current crisis. The handwritten text, addressed to interim party chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan and Secretary General Salman Akram Raja and seen by Dawn , said that the meeting “unanimously” proposed to nominate Mr Gandapur as the acting provincial president in the absence of Junaid Akbar, calling the ex-CM “the right man for the right job”. Their four-pronged agenda included party organisation issues; the status of negotiations with the government; the party’s plan for further protests; and legal issues. The main outcome that invited derision from Mr Raja, however, was the resolution demanding that Mr Gandapur be appointed the acting provincial president immediately. This prompted the secretary general to take a dig at “the narrative” regarding a possible announcement by a group of party MPAs, nominating a new provincial president without permission from their jailed leader Imran Khan, or the party’s political committee. He put the number of these dissidents at 68. Ali Amin Gandapur The secretary general accused the group of cutting off contact with Sohail Afridi and his team in the final days of the protest march, paving the way for state coercion, emergency and governor’s rule in the province. He asserted that Ali Asghar, the party’s provincial general secretary, remained the acting provincial head and Mr Afridi continued to be the chief minister, in accordance with the law and Constitution. “Those spreading doubts — the snakes and the serpents — will be defeated,” he wrote while concluding his post on X. Subsequently, an angry Mr Gandapur took to X to hit back at the secretary general’s claims; in a series of tweets and audio messages, he took strong exception to Mr Raja’s tone and tenor. Demanding that he bring to an end “the spectacle” that had been made of the party, the former KP CM said that the secretary general had no right to accuse others of conspiracy, or call them names like “snakes and serpents”. “Do you understand this? We know how to make others understand if they don’t get this,” he said in an angry tone. Accusing Mr Raja of “hiding” during the party’s protest movement, he asked what sacrifices he had rendered for the party, and demanded the secretary general apologise for his remarks. “At a time when the party is facing unprecedented political challenges, levelling vague accusations and using mocking language against your own elected representatives does not befit responsible leadership,” he wrote on X. “I don’t know who has fed Salman Akram Raja and what the purpose of his tweet was”, Mr Gandapur continued. He also wondered why Mr Raja and Barrister Gohar did not attend parliamentary party meetings, despite repeated invitations to discuss the fallout of the decisions they had taken, which had brought the party to this juncture. “If the parliamentary party of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa wants to seek a constitutional and political solution to the current crisis through consultation within itself, who has given a few individuals the authority to label these elected representatives as traitors, conspirators, or undemocratic?” Incidentally, this is not the first time that both men have taken to social media to air their internal party grievances. In 2025, ahead of a nationwide protest, Mr Gandapur and then-PTI Punjab organiser Aliya Hamza Malik had become embroiled in a similar argument over social media. At the time, the argument had prompted a censure from the jailed party founder, who had strictly instructed senior officeholders and junior members alike to avoid expressing “internal differences on social media, electronic media, print media, or any other platform”. “Publicly airing internal matters or individual concerns before the media is entirely unacceptable,” Imran Khan had said at the time. The latest exchange between the two party leaders also harkened to an outburst from MPA Mashal Yousafzai — former spokesperson to Bushra Bibi — who has blamed the former chief minister and a few other party leaders for the failure of the protest march and subsequent imposition of governor’s rule. Saudis intercept more drones as conflict with Houthis spirals. • Coalition downs six drones launched towards cities, including Madina, as interception debris kills two • Rebels deny ‘deep operations’ in Saudi territory • Iran says Egypt entering Yemen war makes situation ‘more difficult’ • Macron arrives in Riyadh for ‘surprise solidarity visit’ RIYADH: As the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi movement continues to escalate, the Saudi-led coalition on Wednesday said it had intercepted six drones launched towards the kingdom, including in the Madina region. “Four drones launched towards the kingdom have been intercepted and destroyed,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X, adding in a second post that the interceptions took place in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern region as well as Madina. Al-Malki, who did not specify who was behind the launches, later said drones had been intercepted, also in the eastern region. The Houthis denied having targeted the kingdom, with military spokesman Yahya Saree saying their forces had not carried out any “deep” operations in Saudi territory. The Saudi energy ministry said that falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility “resulted in the deaths of two individuals, a Filipino and a Nepali, and injuries to two others”. It did not say who launched the drone aimed at Shaybah oil field near the UAE border. Within Yemen, the Houthis claimed an attack on Wednesday on a military camp near the airport in the southern city of Aden, where the Yemeni government is based. “Our armed forces were able to target the Saudi enemy’s operations room in the Badr camp in Aden with a ballistic missile,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement. A government military source and a local official told Reuters the group also attacked Riyan airport in the southeastern coastal city of Mukalla. “The Houthis used missiles and drones to target a military base housing forces from the Saudi-led coalition at Al Rayyan airport,” one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP. Saree said the group had targeted “military equipment transported by the Saudi enemy via military cargo planes to Al Rayyan airport”. Egypt to support Saudis Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Wednesday that Cairo’s proposed military support for Riyadh was to “defend Saudi territory, and does not include an attack on Yemen,” state-linked media reported. Al-Qahera News , which is closely linked to state intelligence and is to broadcast a speech by Sisi, reported that he also said “the stability of our brothers in the Gulf concerns Egypt’s national security”. The speech itself has not yet been aired by Wednesday night. Egypt’s parliament on Monday delayed a debate on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s request to authorise military support for Saudi Arabia until next week. Sisi had asked lawmakers to approve military support for Saudi Arabia if requested by the kingdom, which has come under near-daily attacks from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis. Iran warns against interference However, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that any interference in the Yemen war by Egypt or any other country would make the situation “more difficult”. “Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict,” said Iran’s top diplomat in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya aired on Tuesday. “We believe that any foreign presence or interference will only make resolving this issue more difficult,” Mr Araghchi noted. He added that Egypt has said it “will not enter Yemen or engage in a war against Yemen”. The decade-plus war between the Iran-backed Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government reignited in July. Macron meets MbS Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron arrived in Riyadh in a surprise “solidarity” visit, and met Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Macron is the first Western leader to visit since the Houthis intensified their attacks on the kingdom this month. The trip is part of a Gulf tour to secure diesel and petrol supplies as Macron seeks to bring down energy prices following violent protests in France sparked by rising living costs that have created a political crisis for the president. ‘Letting roots of Pak-India conflict fester invites more danger’. ISLAMABAD: Failure to address the underlying disputes that engender crises between Pakistan and India could lead to more dangerous confrontations in the future, a former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee warned on Wednesday. “Terminating a crisis without addressing its root causes only sets the stage for the next, more dangerous conflict,” retired Gen Zubair Mahmood Hayat said at the concluding session of the second Islamabad Non-Proliferation Conference, organised by the Strategic Vision Institute (SVI). Ex-CJCSC warns against ignoring Kashmir dispute, Indus treaty suspension He said that in the subcontinent, the core issue of Jammu and Kashmir could not be wished away or reduced to an administrative matter. “Similarly, water cannot be converted from a shared necessity into an instrument of power and pressure,” he said while stressing the need for resolution of the Kashmir dispute and restoration of the Indus Waters Treaty. Gen Hayat warned that repeated crises between the nuclear-armed neighbours could become increasingly dangerous if unresolved disputes, diminishing restraint and the absence of sustained political dialogue continued to undermine regional security. Referring to the May 2025 conflict , he said Pakistan had demonstrated its military capabilities and political control through a calibrated response that denied India a unilateral fait accompli without pursuing an unlimited war. “The larger lesson is not that conflict between two nuclear-armed neighbours can be made routine; it is that there is no tested and certified safe space for war,” he said, warning that future crises would involve different leaders, emerging technologies and shorter decision-making timelines, heightening the risk of miscalculation. He said South Asia lacked an inclusive regional security framework, effective crisis-management mechanisms and sustained political dialogue. “The region lives between deterrence that prevents the worst and disputes that repeatedly regenerate danger,” he said. Gen Hayat warned unverified allegations could trigger conflict before the facts were established, with a future confrontation potentially arising from an accident rather than a deliberate state decision.
