Maldives president, CDF Munir stress importance of strengthening defence cooperation. Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and visiting Maldivian President Dr Mohamed Muizzu underscored the importance of strengthening bilateral defence cooperation on Wednesday, state-run Radio Pakistan reported . Muizzu arrived in Islamabad on Tuesday on a three-day visit at the invitation of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. The visit marks the first by a Maldivian president to Pakistan in 11 years, and comes as the two countries celebrate the 60th anniversary of their diplomatic relations, established in 1966. CDF Munir called on the visiting president in Islamabad, where the two leaders discussed matters of mutual interest, the prevailing regional security environment, and avenues for enhancing bilateral cooperation, the Radio Pakistan report said. “Both sides underscored the importance of strengthening defence cooperation, institutional linkages and professional exchanges,” it added. The CDF highlighted the “longstanding and cordial relations” between the two countries. He reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to further strengthening bilateral cooperation and promoting peace, stability and security in the region through constructive engagement, Radio Pakistan said. It added that President Muizzu commended the professionalism of Pakistan’s armed forces and appreciated the country’s continued efforts to promote regional peace and stability. PM Shehbaz vows strengthening of bilateral relations Earlier, PM Shehbaz vowed to strengthen bilateral relations with the Maldives, as the two countries signed 20 memorandums of understanding (MoUs). Addressing a joint press stakeout following the signing of 20 wide-ranging MoUs, PM Shehbaz said, “There is no doubt that the two countries [will] keep on strengthening these relations for all time to come.” The premier extended a “very warm welcome” to the visiting dignitary and his delegation. PM Shehbaz expressed his “warmest greetings and heartfelt affection to the people of Dhivehi Raajje, the land of islands, a nation whose spirit is as vast as the ocean that surrounds it,” hailing 60 years of diplomatic ties between the two countries. The prime minister noted that he and Muizzu, in their bilateral and delegation-level talks, discussed “all important issues which have direct bearing between our two brotherly countries and of course, regional and international issues”. “I am very happy to announce that we had a wonderful session, very productive and very fruitful discussions,” he remarked. PM Shehbaz noted that the conversations encompassed “economic and trade relations, our strategic defence cooperation, our support for training of our brothers and sisters from Maldives in Pakistan in various walks of life; police, defence, education, health and many other” fields. The prime minister went on to announce that both sides had agreed to raise their bilateral trade from $13.9 million — “just a fraction of our potential” — to $200m in the next two years. Highlighting that the two South Asian countries had “very strong” relations, coupled with a “long list of mutual achievements”, PM Shehbaz said both sides noted that their ties “do not reflect the true strength of our economic cooperation”. Thanking Muizzu for his “personal support in this behalf”, the premier went on to announce that Islamabad would support Malé in promoting the plantation of 5m trees in the Maldives by providing 100,000 olive cuttings and 100,000 seeds of various plant species within a mutually decided timeframe. Referring to the MoUs signed, he affirmed that he “will be very happy to personally work with [Muizzu] to translate these written MoUs into action with prompt decision-making and speedy implementation”. The prime minister declared that Pakistan was “absolutely ready to provide technical expertise to various segments of our mutual cooperation and, above all, Pakistan is very happy to learn that Maldives is moving forward speedily to establish data centres in other places”. “This is great news, and as a matter of good luck, Pakistan has also attained a reasonable level of expertise and professional capability in this field,” he added, noting that the country had set up data centres in various locations. He offered Pakistan’s “experience and our professional capabilities in this behalf” to the Maldives. PM Shehbaz noted that a large number of Maldivian students were receiving education in Pakistani universities and colleges, particularly in the field of healthcare, and that 250 Pakistani doctors and other paramedics were serving in the Maldives. “This shall continue in future with bigger numbers so that whatever requirements you have, we as a brotherly country would be more than happy to fulfil those requirements willingly and with utmost sincerity of purpose,” the prime minister said. Speaking on international developments, PM Shehbaz commended the Maldives’ “unwavering” support for the Palestinian cause, adding that Islamabad remains fully committed to the Palestinians’ right of self-determination and the establishment of an independent state of Palestine. The premier further said he briefed Muizzu on Pakistan’s principled position on occupied Jammu and Kashmir, declaring Islamabad’s support for a peaceful resolution of the dispute in accordance with the relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions. “Till they have won their struggle and gotten the right of self-determination, Pakistan shall continue to support them diplomatically and, of course, support them at all international forums till they become an independent sovereign country as per UNSC resolutions, and their sacrifice will not go to waste at all,” he said. The prime minister also expressed Pakistan’s “serious concern” over India’s decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance in April 2025, pointing out that it was a violation of an international binding treaty. “Pakistan’s position is loud and clear and beyond an array of doubt; legally binding treaties must be respected and shared water resources must never be weaponised or used as an instrument of political pressure or blackmailing,” he stated. PM Shehbaz said Pakistan has made it “abundantly clear at various forums ”, including the UN General Assembly last month, that water was a “red line” for the country. “Waterflows in any canal or ocean, sea or straits, carries trade, commerce, message of prosperity and progress, and not threats, confrontations and conflicts,” he said. “Water is a lifeline for humanity […] so this should be known to all and sundry that any violation in this behalf will be regarded by Pakistan as an act of war,” the prime minister warned. Concluding his remarks, PM Shehbaz said Muizzu’s visit had given Pakistan-Maldives relations “new purpose and new momentum”. He remarked, “The same ocean that touches the shores of Karachi and Gwadar embraces the islands of the Maldives. “For centuries, its waves have carried traders, scholars and travellers between our lands. Today, they carry the renewed promise of our wonderful friendship whose finest chapters are yet to be written.” In his comments, Muizzu appreciated PM Shehbaz, the government and people of Pakistan for “their exceptional warmth and gracious hospitality”. He added that his visit coming on the 60-year mark of Pakistan-Maldives diplomatic relations made it “particularly significant”. The 60 years have been marked by warmth, friendship and shared perspectives, he said. “This visit takes place after a decade-long interval. It offers us an important opportunity not simply to celebrate the friendship of the past but to define the partnership of the future,” Muizzu said. Stressing on the close relations between the two countries, he said, “Only two such longstanding friends could have talked so widely and agreed on so much about our future together”. Muizzu said, for him, the talks represented a “clear shared ambition to move the Maldives-Pakistan partnership into a new era”. He said the discussions encompassed several sectors including trade and investment; health and education; environment, fisheries and agriculture; youth and sports; policing and defence; training and capacity-building; and tourism. The Maldivian president said he was pleased about the signing of 20 MoUs. “These memoranda will open new avenues for cooperation among multiple sectors, but agreements are meaningful only when they produce results. Our next step, of course, is to translate these understandings into tangible opportunities and meaningful benefits for the people of both nations.” Muizzu also said he endorsed the goal to take the two countries’ bilateral trade quantum from $13m to $200m in two years. “The Maldives and Pakistan are worlds of untapped potential for each other,” the Maldivian president said. He reaffirmed that the two countries would take a “firm step in the right direction”, adding that Thursday’s business forum would provide an opportunity to bring together business leaders, inventors and innovators from both countries to turn the friendship into mutually beneficial investments. He said he was encouraged by the discussions to establish direct flights between Pakistan and the Maldives, adding that direct flights would help support tourism as well. He further said that the two countries’ leaders saw “considerable potential in halal and Muslim-friendly tourism”. Moreover, Muizzu appreciated Pakistan’s scholarships and placements for Maldivian students, adding that the leaders would broaden the opportunities further, especially in artificial intelligence, digitisation and future technologies as well as health. “We want our next generation to be prepared for the future and be prepared to shape that future.” Muizzu stressed that climate change was “not an abstract environmental concern” for the Maldives, but “it is a direct challenge to our security, our development and our future”. He welcomed cooperation with Pakistan in areas of climate resilience, conservation, sustainable waste management and renewable energy. He thanked PM Shehbaz for his announcement of donations to help the Maldives plant 5m trees in five years. “Our nations share a commitment to advancing common interests through constructive engagements.” He said the Maldives remained committed to revitalising the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, adding that “rebuilding trust, encouraging meaningful dialogue and strengthening mutual understanding are essential to unlocking the full potential of regional cooperation”. He further expressed the Maldives’ “unequivocal and steadfast solidarity” with Palestinians and their “legitimate right to self-determination”. Muizzu also commended Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts “to promote dialogue, de-escalation, humanitarian assistance and a just and lasting peace” in the Middle East. Concluding his remarks, he said, “For 60 years, Pakistan has stood as a trusted friend of the Maldives.” The two countries have now agreed to “build a new era of partnership on the foundations of our six decades of friendship”, he said. The Maldivian president was later conferred with an honorary doctorate in politics by the International Islamic University Islamabad, with PM Shehbaz noting that the degree recognised Muizzu’s “sagacious and wise leadership and your great public service to your people in the Maldives”. 20 MoUs signed Pakistan and the Maldives signed a series of MoUs aimed at deepening bilateral relations in multiple sectors, including defence, IT, cybersecurity, health, education, social protection, agriculture and tourism, among others. PM Shehbaz and Muizzu were present at the ceremony where representatives from both sides exchanged the pre-signed documents. The two countries signed an MoU on cooperation in the fields of information technology, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, digital skills, and technology and innovation. An MoU was inked to strengthen cooperation in combating illicit trafficking and abuse of narcotic drugs. The two sides also signed an MoU on social protection as well as on health cooperation and between Maldives Food and Drug Authority and the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan. Both nations also signed MoUs focused on the recruitment of health professionals, strengthening defence ties and maritime security cooperation. An MoU was signed to boost agriculture cooperation, besides another one on promoting fisheries cooperation. To promote ties in technical and vocational education, an MoU on collaboration to promote technical and vocational education and training was signed, while another MoU was inked to promote educational cooperation. The representatives of Pakistan and the Maldives also exchanged MoUs on cooperation in the field of youth and sports development, air connectivity, tourism and in the field of arts, culture and heritage. The MoUs were signed between the National College of Policy and Law Enforcement of the Maldives Police Service and National Police Academy, Islamabad; Civil Service Commission of Maldives and the Federal Public Service Commission of Pakistan; and Civil Service Commission of Maldives and Civil Service Academy (CSA) of Pakistan. In order to boost commercial engagement, an MoU was signed between the Maldives State Trading Organisation (STO) and Trading Corporation of Pakistan (TCP) for cooperation in trade of agriculture commodities, food and other products, besides signing another pact aimed at boosting cooperation in the field of environment. Prior to the MoU signing ceremony, Muizzi was welcomed at the Prime Minister House with a guard of honour. He held introductions with federal ministers while PM Shehbaz greeted the Maldivian delegation. According to a statement by PM Office (PMO), the prime minister extended a “warm welcome to the esteemed guest”, followed by a guard of honour by smartly turned-out contingents of all three armed forces. The visiting dignitary also planted a sapling at PM House, and prayers were offered for the progress and prosperity of both countries. A Pakistan-Maldives Business Forum will also be held during the visit to promote interaction between the two countries’ business communities and explore opportunities for trade and investment. President Zardari calls for stronger bilateral economic cooperation President Zardari also met his Maldivian counterpart at the President’s House in Islamabad, where he emphasised the need to translate the political goodwill between the two countries into “greater trade, investment, connectivity and people-to-people exchanges”. According to a press release by the President’s Secretariat, he also reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to supporting Maldives in education, healthcare, human resource development, social protection and sustainable development. “The two leaders reviewed bilateral relations and discussed ways to strengthen cooperation in areas of mutual interest,” the statement said. President Zardari reaffirmed the importance Pakistan attaches to its “longstanding fraternal relations” with the Maldives, highlighting that Muizzu’s state visit coincided with the 60-year anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries and provided “fresh momentum” to the bilateral partnership. He also recalled Pakistan’s contributions to the development of the Maldives, including the Parliament building and the School of Medicine in Malé. The press release added that both leaders expressed satisfaction over the positive trajectory of bilateral relations and reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation in areas of mutual interest. They recognised the disproportionate impact of climate change on vulnerable countries, particularly small island developing states and climate-vulnerable developing economies. “President Zardari expressed Pakistan’s readiness to deepen cooperation with Maldives in climate resilience, environmental protection and sustainable development, including support for President Muizzu’s Five Million Tree Initiative,” the statement said. Additionally, the leaders exchanged views on regional and international developments and underscored the importance of “dialogue, diplomacy, sovereign equality, mutual respect and peaceful resolution of disputes”, it said. They also reaffirmed their support for the rights of the Palestinian people and the establishment of an independent and sovereign State of Palestine. According to the statement, Muizzu was accompanied by Maldivian Foreign Minister Iruthisham Adam; Minister of Defence and National Service Hassan Rasheed; Minister of Homeland Security, Labour and Technology Ali Ihusaan; Minister of Economic Development, Transport and Trade Mohamed Saeed; and High Commissioner of the Republic of Maldives Mohamed Thoha. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Maritime Minister Junaid Anwar, Senators Sherry Rehman and Saleem Mandviwala, former federal minister MNA Naveed Qamar, the foreign secretary, and the High Commissioner of Pakistan to the Maldives were also present, it added. The meeting was followed by a state banquet hosted by President Zardari in honour of President Muizzu and his accompanying delegation. It was attended, among others, by PM Shehbaz, CDF Munir, Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf, Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Baber Sidhu and Commander National Strategic Command General Syed Aamer Raza. Meeting with Dar Earlier in the day, DPM Dar called on Muizzu, welcoming him and his delegation to Pakistan, the FO said on X. Dar “underscored the importance of expanding bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade, investment, education, climate change and tourism”, the FO said. DPM Dar also welcomed the Maldivian business delegation in the Maldives-Pakistan Business Forum and “expressed hope that B2B engagements would yield concrete trade and investment opportunities”. Muizzu, speaking to Dar, “expressed Maldives’ desire to deepen its close relations with Pakistan and explore new avenues of mutually beneficial cooperation”, the FO said. Separately, Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry held a meeting with Maldivian Minister for Homeland Security Ali Ihusan and exchanged views on enhancing bilateral relations and cooperation between the two countries, a statement by the interior ministry said. According to the statement, the two agreed to promote cooperation on immigration and to curb human smuggling and organised crime. It quoted Chaudhry as saying: “Pakistan values sharing experiences and security cooperation with friendly countries to promote peace and stability in the region. Pakistan wants to strengthen bilateral cooperation with the Maldives in the areas of law enforcement and internal security.” He stressed the need for cooperation between the two sides to tackle the challenges of illegal immigration and human smuggling and assured the visiting dignitary on Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s behalf of “all-possible assistance for enhancing bilateral cooperation”. Last month, the Maldives’ parliamentary speaker Abdul Raheem Abdullah met with Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir in Rawalpindi. In 2015 , former Maldivian president Abdulla Yameen Abdul Gayoom undertook a two-day state visit to Pakistan on May 6-7 at the invitation of then-PM Nawaz Sharif.

Lahore Gymkhana’s low rent attributed to ‘decades of oversight failures’. LAHORE: A special committee of the Punjab Assembly, chaired by MPA Samiullah Khan, came down hard on decades of government oversight failures after Lahore Gymkhana Club Chairman Salman Siddique conceded that the annual rent of Rs5,000 paid for over 100 acres of prime state land in the provincial capital was wholly inadequate. Appearing before the committee alongside members of the club’s management, Mr Siddique expressed surprise at the nominal rate given the vast acreage involved and the club’s vastly improved financial footing. Contrasting the institution’s current financial standing with its constraints during the 1990s, he admitted that the club should be paying at least Rs10 million annually, while expressing willingness to cooperate with the ongoing inquiry and share records. Committee members noted that this admission from the club’s own top leadership underscored the urgency of determining why successive state authorities allowed such a massive concession to persist without meaningful scrutiny. They stressed that the onus rested squarely on public institutions mandated to protect state land, enforce lease terms, and ensure transparent usage. During the session, the member colonies of the board of revenue revealed that then chief minister Sardar Muhammad Arif Nakai, who was also a member of the club, had verbally directed the fixation of a token Rs5,000 annual rent for the lease extension in 1996, bypassing proper land valuation and relevant legal principles. Perturbed by how a mere verbal instruction could underpin such a major agreement, lawmakers demanded the complete documentary record detailing the legal authority and approval process behind the 1996 lease deed. PA body constitutes fact-finding committee to frame specific queries, verify records, and present comprehensive report within 10 days Emphasising that the land ultimately belongs to the people of Punjab, the committee was presented with estimates valuing the prime property between Rs76 billion and Rs218 billion. Members questioned the state’s failure to secure a fair public return on an asset of this scale and firmly rejected any notion that the club’s internal corporate governance shielded it from state oversight, maintaining that institutional autonomy cannot supersede accountability for public property. Touching upon structural approvals, Mr Siddique affirmed that while the club fulfills its corporate and tax obligations under the Companies Act 2017, he has struggled to locate internal records regarding official building sanctions. In response, lawmakers called for strict verification of sanctioned building plans, statutory permissions, and compliance with lease terms, raising safety concerns over structures lacking documented approvals. On the issue of an independent state audit, Mr Siddique noted that the matter remains pending before the Supreme Court and assured adherence to its eventual verdict, a position echoed by management committee member Tasneem Noorani. The panel also explored proposals aimed at broader public utility, such as opening the club’s cricket ground to the general public or relocating the facility near the Ring Road, while questioning why public funds were ever spent on an exclusive recreational club occupying state land. To take the probe forward, the committee directed the Lahore Development Authority, Parks and Horticulture Authority, Federal Board of Revenue, and other relevant bodies to submit detailed jurisdictional reports. Furthermore, a fact-finding committee headed by the Advocate General Punjab, comprising officials from the Board of Revenue, Metropolitan Corporation Lahore, Law department, Agriculture department, and the deputy commissioner, had been assigned to frame specific queries, verify records, and present a comprehensive report within ten days. Concluding the session, the chairperson directed that legal questions stemming from the proceedings be forwarded to the high-powered Law Reforms Committee, headed by Speaker Malik Muhammad Ahmad Khan, for joint deliberations aimed at fixing responsibility for oversight lapses and ensuring the lawful use of public land. Published in Dawn, October 22nd, 2026

Noor Zaman stuns defending champion Gawad to reach Silicon Valley Open quarters. Pakistan’s Noor Zaman stunned defending champion and world No. 4 Karim Abdel Gawad of Egypt 3-1 on Wednesday to reach the quarter-finals of the PSA Gold Silicon Valley Open at the Redwood City in California. The 22-year-old overcame the second seed 11-9, 11-7, 9-11, 11-6 in 52 minutes at Squash Zone, handing the Egyptian a shock defeat in the $143,500 men’s event. “I was ready mentally and physically today, and I think now is the time for me to beat the top players,” Noor said after the match. Noor, ranked among the world’s top 35 players, had earlier booked his place in the last 16 with a 3-1 victory over American wildcard Bransten Ming. After losing the opening game 3-11, he fought back to win 11-5, 11-8, 11-9 in 41 minutes. The Peshawar-born player, grandson of former world champion Qamar Zaman and the 2025 U-23 world champion, has enjoyed a strong run of form in recent months, climbing into the world’s top 30 and collecting five PSA titles. Meanwhile, Pakistan’s Mohammad Ashab Irfan bowed out in the last 16 after losing 3-0 to fifth seed Mohamed ElShorbagy of Egypt. Irfan had reached the round with a straight-games victory over Hungary’s Balazs Farkas, winning 11-6, 11-4, 11-5. The PSA World Tour Gold event offers equal prize money for men and women as squash prepares for its Olympic debut at Los Angeles 2028.

Suspects in West Bank settler attacks put under house arrest. All but one of the suspects arrested over recent settler attacks on an American photojournalist and a visiting French mayor in the West Bank have been released from detention and placed under house arrest, their lawyers said. Israeli police had announced on Monday the arrests of 10 people implicated in the attacks in the occupied Palestinian territory, where violence by Israeli settlers is on the rise but perpetrators are seldom prosecuted. Honenu, a legal aid organisation that often represents Israeli soldiers and settlers, said that all but one of the suspects had been released to house arrest. Lawyer Assaf Gonen said in a statement that their arrests had only been “for show”, and were “intended to satisfy media pressure and foreign interests”. The suspects have not been identified. On Friday, photographer Heidi Levine, 65, who was on assignment for T he Washington Post , was taken to hospital with broken vertebrae after being beaten by settlers while covering the West Bank’s annual olive harvest. The incident comes 10 days after settlers beat an AFP photographer covering the West Bank olive harvest , Jaafar Ashtiyeh, leaving him also requiring hospital treatment. A day later, settlers attacked a convoy of European diplomats and beat up Bernard Baudoux, 78, the mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries who was on a goodwill visit. The attacks drew international condemnation, but mixed messages from the Israeli government. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is facing a tight race for a new mandate, has tried to shore up his pro-settlement right-wing base and has cast doubt on the circumstances behind the recent settler attacks on Westerners. His tone has drawn unusually strong criticism from the opposition, which has accused him of tarnishing Israel’s image. Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank, with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians. Settlers have also been seizing olive groves owned by Palestinians, who see the trees as a cultural symbol. Excluding east Jerusalem, around three million Palestinians live in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, alongside more than 500,000 Israelis residing in settlements considered illegal under international law.

LHC issues notices to foreign secretary in contempt cases over detention of PTI-linked Pakistanis in UAE. LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Thursday issued notices to Foreign Secretary Asim Iftikhar in two separate contempt petitions over alleged non-compliance with an earlier court order concerning two PTI-affiliated Pakistani citizens detained in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). On September 14, the LHC had directed the foreign secretary to process and decide within 15 days representations concerning the detention of two citizens — Syed Salman Raza Zaidi and Muhammad Junaid Jahangir. Justice Sadiq Mehmood Khurram heard the contempt petitions on Thursday. Barrister Abuzar Salman Niazi appeared on behalf of the petitioners and alleged that the two individuals remained deprived of consular, diplomatic, and legal access. He recalled the court’s Sept 14 directive and contended that the petitioners had not been formally informed of any decision on their representations, even though a considerable amount of time had passed. The counsel urged the court to initiate contempt proceedings against the foreign secretary for non-compliance. After hearing initial arguments, Justice Khurram issued notices to the respondent secretary for submission of his reply by October 29. In the main petitions, the counsel stated that Zaidi went missing from his residence in Sharjah on Sept 27, 2024, and was subsequently taken into custody by UAE authorities. He said despite nearly two years having passed, the petitioner, Faryal Zainab, had still not been provided clear information regarding the charges against her husband Zaidi, the judicial proceedings, any sentence, or the complete court record. Meanwhile, Advocate Niazi said Jahangir was allegedly detained on Sept 24, 2024, at Dubai airport on his return from Saudi Arabia. Muhammad Ibrahim, Jahangir’s father, filed the petition challenging the alleged failure of the federal government and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) to provide effective consular protection and legal assistance. The counsel for the petitioners submitted that despite representations having been filed regarding the detention of both citizens before the foreign secretary, the representations had not been processed. Both petitioners had asked the court to direct that legal and consular assistance be provided to Zaidi and Jahangir, that their judicial records be obtained and that diplomatic-level steps be taken toward their return to Pakistan.

IMF sees 1.3pc contraction in Pakistan this year due to Iran war. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Thursday forecast a sharp drop in economic output in Pakistan, the Middle East and North Africa this year due to the US-Israeli-led war against Iran , followed by a rebound to 6.6 per cent growth in 2027, while warning that further energy production disruptions could worsen the outlook. The IMF said the region’s output was expected to contract by 1.3pc as a result of the war’s impact on energy production, shipping, tourism, trade and confidence. Economic output would increase sharply in 2027, but output in those economies would generally stay below pre-war projections. The war’s impact had been substantial, but uneven, with oil-exporting economies directly affected by disruptions to energy production and shipping hit harder, and oil importers proving to be more resilient, the IMF said in its regional outlook released Thursday in Dubai. The IMF said its baseline assumed that the conflict would abate in early 2027 and that trade would gradually normalise during the year, but it said the outlook remained clouded by “exceptionally high uncertainty.” “The main risks derive from further disruption to energy production and trade routes that could drive energy prices higher,” the IMF said in a statement outlining its key messages, noting external financial conditions could also tighten. External financial conditions could also tighten if investors reassess AI-driven productivity gains and interest rates rise further amid heightened concerns about inflation and fiscal positions, it said. Oil importers had proven more resilient, with domestic demand supported by remittances and tourism flows, favourable financial conditions, and prompt policy responses that safeguard consumers from higher commodity prices, the IMF said. Growth in the Caucasus and Central Asia was moderating toward a more sustainable pace, the IMF said, forecasting a 5.2pc rise in economic output in 2026 and 5pc in 2027. The IMF underscored the mantra it delivered during last week’s annual meetings, urging policymakers to prioritise maintaining price stability, while preserving fiscal sustainability, maintaining central bank independence and enacting structural reforms to boost productivity and create jobs.

Karachi judicial magistrate rejects bail plea of anchorperson Iqrarul Hassan. KARACHI: A local court on Thursday rejected TV anchorperson Iqrarul Hassan’s bail plea in a cybercrime case pertaining to the alleged dissemination of anti-state content. Hassan was arrested last week for allegedly disseminating anti-state, false and defamatory content through his official social media accounts. He was booked under multiple sections of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca). According to an order issued by the judicial magistrate, a copy of which is available with Dawn , “the order disposes of the bail application filed under Section 497 of the CrPC on behalf of the applicant/accused, Syed Iqrar Ul Hassan, son of Syed Muhammad Ismail, who has been arrested in connection with FIR No. 101/2026 registered at Police Station NCCIA, Cyber Crime Reporting Centre, Karachi, under Sections 9, 10, 20, 24 and 26-A of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016 (as amended in 2025)”. The notice of the bail application was served on the NCCIA’s additional director (legal), the order states. Earlier this week, Hassan was sent to prison on judicial remand after the NCCIA sought an extension of his physical remand by another eight days. However, Karachi (East) Judicial Magistrate-I Gulraiz Memon observed that the agency had been given “sufficient time of physical custody”. “No cogent reason has been given by NCCIA for extension of physical custody; therefore, the accused is remanded to judicial custody till Oct 26,” the judge stated in his order. The court also issued notices to the NCCIA on a bail application filed by Hassan’s defence counsel, Barrister Mian Ali Ashfaq, and fixed the matter for hearing on Oct 21. On Oct 17, Hassan was produced before Judicial Magistrate Memon upon the completion of his initial four-day physical remand. The NCCIA sought a further 10 days of custody for questioning, but the magistrate rejected the request and granted the agency two more days. The magistrate also dismissed a plea filed by Hassan’s counsel under Section 63 of the CrPC seeking his discharge from the case. In its remand report, the NCCIA said the investigation had progressed but several important aspects remained to be examined in light of the forensic analysis of Hassan’s seized digital devices and records from other departments, including the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra). The agency said digital devices containing 1,145.89 gigabytes of data had been handed over to its forensic team for analysis to identify relevant applications, social media accounts, email accounts, stored files and communications linked to the alleged content. The NCCIA also sought further custody to trace the “origin, relation, financial correlation and cross-border linkages (if any)” of the posts. In his earlier order, the magistrate observed that collecting digital footprints, technical data and forensic evidence required reasonable time, adding that discharging an accused while the investigation was under way could hamper the process. The NCCIA alleged that the content was intended to incite the public against constitutional implementation and could cause panic, disorder and unrest. Hassan was booked under sections 9 (glorification of an offence), 10 (cyberterrorism), 24 (cyberstalking) and 26A (Punishment for false and fake information) of Peca. He had been critical of the government’s policies on social media.

LHC summons Punjab home secretary, Kot Lakhpat jail superintendent in plea seeking release of Imran’s sisters. LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Thursday summoned the Punjab home secretary and the superintendent of Kot Lakhpat jail in connection with a petition seeking the release of former prime minister Imran Khan’s three sisters. Imran’s sisters — Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Uzma Khan — were detained by authorities in September, under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960, as the PTI geared up for a planned protest march towards Islamabad. Their detention was ordered for 30 days. A day earlier, Aleema’s son, Shahrez Khan, filed a fresh plea challenging their detention. It stated that Imran’s sisters remained at Lahore’s Kot Lakhpat jail despite the lapse of the 30-day period of their detention. Justice Abher Gul Khan took up the petition on Thursday. Advocate Rana Mudassar Umar appeared on behalf of the petitioner and submitted that the detention orders of the three sisters had expired on Oct 19 and 20, but they had not been released. Justice Khan asked the counsel why he had not made the Lahore deputy commissioner a respondent in the petition. The counsel replied that the deputy commissioner had not been impleaded because the detention notification issued by the official had expired. Uzma’s husband, Ahad Khan, also approached the rostrum and requested the court to summon the deputy commissioner. The judge, however, observed that the official could not be summoned as he had not been made a party to the petition. Subsequently, the court adjourned the hearing until Oct 28 and directed the home secretary and the jail superintendent to appear in person along with their reports on the matter. In Wednesday’s petition, Shahrez contended that the detention period had expired, but the three sisters remained in custody. He asked the court to order their release. It was argued that their detention was a consequence of their efforts for their brother’s release. It further contended that the preventive detention could not replace ordinary criminal law and that the order violated Article 10 as well as the safeguards of Section 3 of the MPO. The petitioner requested the court to direct the jail superintendent to produce the detainees before the court and “set them at liberty, in the interest of justice, equity and fair play”. The petitioner asked the court to declare the detention orders void and issue directives for the detainees’ release, while suspending the operation of the orders.

New Delhi steps up air pollution controls ahead of winter. India began annual measures on Thursday to tackle toxic air pollution in New Delhi, a megacity of 30 million people regularly ranked among the world’s most polluted capitals. Delhi’s air quality deteriorates in winter, when cooler air traps pollutants close to the ground. Major sources include coal-fired power plants, traffic, construction and farm stubble burning in neighbouring areas. The Delhi government on Wednesday announced a ban on open rubbish burning and ordered food stalls to stop using coal or firewood. In previous years, such measures have failed to curb pollution, which peaks from November to January, when levels of cancer-causing PM 2.5 microparticles often hit more than 300 micrograms per cubic metre, 20 times the World Health Organisation’s recommended daily maximum. Monitors recorded 233 micrograms per cubic metre early on Thursday, about 15 times the limit. The government’s Commission for Air Quality Management has predicted air quality to remain “poor” in the coming days. A study in The Lancet Planetary Health in 2024 estimated that 3.8m deaths in India between 2009 and 2019 were linked to pollution that exceeded India’s own air quality guidelines. Last year, pollution levels peaked at 846 micrograms per cubic metre, 56 times the WHO limit. The UN children’s agency warns that polluted air puts children at heightened risk of acute respiratory infections. Further restrictions take effect on November 1, including doubled parking fees and work-from-home arrangements for government office staff, aimed at reducing traffic emissions. Tighter construction rules will also begin then, followed by a complete ban on construction and demolition from Dec 10 to Jan 20. Last month, the authorities also imposed a construction ban that will run from Dec 10 to Jan 20 as part of a winter action plan to tackle pollution. It will include restrictions on vehicular traffic aimed at encouraging residents to use public transport.

Faster reforms could triple Pakistan’s incomes by 2050, says World Bank. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan’s incomes could triple by 2050 if the country ensures faster implementation of structural reforms, according to the World Bank Group’s latest Pakistan Development Update, titled Attaining Escape Velocity. The report says that following progress on macroeconomic stabilisation, Pakistan has an opportunity to achieve faster and sustained economic growth and create more jobs. Sound macroeconomic policies in recent years have helped stabilise the economy and preserve growth despite the impact of the Middle East conflict . Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth increased to 3.7 per cent in FY26 from 3.2pc in FY25. Revenue growth and expenditure restraint supported record primary fiscal surpluses, which reached 2.9pc of GDP in FY26, while strong remittances enabled the country to rebuild its foreign exchange reserves. These improvements were recognised through upgrades by two major international rating agencies, S&P and Moody’s , and enabled Pakistan to return to international debt markets with the issuance of a $3 billion Eurobond. “Pakistan has made real progress in restoring stability, and markets have taken notice,” World Bank Country Dir­ector Bolormaa Amgaa­baz­­ar said. “But real per capita growth — the rate at which the income of the average Pakistani increases — remains stuck at around 1.6pc. Reforms to drive faster growth are now urgently needed,” she added. The report finds that higher growth is possible if Pakistan follows the path taken by other successful countries in pursuing ambitious economic reforms. Upgrading policies and institutions to the standards of the average middle-income country could drive sustained annual growth of 6.2pc to 6.9pc, allowing Pakistan to reach Vietnam’s current income level by 2050. “With macro stabilisation achieved but fiscal resources and foreign exchange still tightly constrained, structural reform to encourage private investment is the necessary next step towards higher living standards,” said Sebastian Essl, the report’s lead author. “Achieving this kind of private-sector-led growth requires a plan, coordination, and committed reform implementation,” he added. The report outlines an ambitious set of reforms that could enable Pakistan to attain by 2050 the per capita income levels of countries currently at the upper-middle-income threshold. Many of the proposed measures build on reforms already underway. These include timely adjustments to power-sector tariffs, which helped reduce energy subsidies from 1.1pc of GDP in FY25 to 0.8pc in FY26, continued trade liberalisation under the National Tariff Policy and the recent privatisation of Pakistan International Airlines (PIA). Building on these measures, sustained progress will depend on further reforms to improve the business environment, overhaul the tax system, reduce the state’s presence in the economy and expand access to finance.

Pakistan, EU agree to strengthen counterterrorism cooperation at multilateral forums. Pakistan and the European Union (EU) have agreed to strengthen cooperation at multilateral forums, including the United Nations, to advance a coherent counterterrorism approach, according to a statement issued by the Foreign Office (FO) on Thursday. The agreement was reached during the 10th round of the Pakistan-EU Bilateral Counterterrorism Dialogue, held in Islamabad. The Pakistani delegation was led by Dr Fareha Bugti, director general (counterterrorism), while the EU side was headed by Anna Strazska, the European External Action Service’s special envoy for counterterrorism. During the meeting, the two sides exchanged views on recent regional and global developments affecting the terrorism threat landscape and unequivocally condemned terrorism in all its forms, reaffirming their commitment to combating the threat. According to FO, the EU condemned recent terrorist attacks in Pakistan, expressed solidarity with the suffering of affected civilians and recognised the value of Pakistan’s efforts to combat terrorism. “Acknowledging each other’s role in the ongoing global fight against terrorism, Pakistan and the EU expressed concern at the security implications of the situation in Afghanistan,” the statement added. The two sides maintained that effective multilateralism remained essential to building lasting international consensus on terrorism. The discussions also addressed the evolving nature of terrorist threats, including the exploitation of cyberspace and information and energy resources to advance their objectives, the statement said. The FO said Pakistan and the EU exchanged best practices on preventing and countering violent extremism, terrorism financing and radicalisation in all forms, particularly the use of cyberspace by terrorists. It added that the “two sides identified priority areas for cooperation and reaffirmed their commitment to regular, institutionalised engagement on counterterrorism”. The FO said the next round of the dialogue would be held in Brussels at a mutually convenient date next year. The dialogue comes as Pakistan’s counterterrorism challenge enters a new and more complex phase, with terrorist groups evolving their methods of financing and recruitment. On Tuesday, an international seminar on Pakistan’s evolving counterterrorism landscape, organised by the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad, highlighted the changing methods of terrorist groups, including their financing and recruitment. PM vows to bring back progress to KP, assails PTI's 'callousness' during its tenures. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday vowed that the federal government, which now runs Khyber Pakhtunkhwa under governor’s rule, would make every effort possible to “bring back” progress to the province. He made the remarks while chairing a meeting of the provincial apex committee in Peshawar, where he arrived earlier in the day on his first visit to the province since the imposition of governor’s rule and the declaration of an emergency on Oct 11. The meeting, attended by Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, reviewed KP’s overall security situation. Federal ministers and newly appointed provincial advisers were also present. Addressing the committee, PM Shehbaz reiterated that emergency and governor’s rule had to be imposed “under extreme compulsion”. He stated: “I promise that we will leave no stone unturned in bringing back the happiness and era of progress to this province, and in the practical realisation of the wishes, aspirations, and dreams of this province’s people that have been shattered due to the worst actions of recent years.” The prime minister affirmed that the Centre “will place all possible resources at your feet”. He added that the Advisory Council led by the governor, he, the president and the CDF “will ensure that this province, once again, not only matches the other provinces in the race for development, but I would be extremely happy if it moves even further ahead”. The prime minister regretted that “terrorists were summoned back here” after peace had been established, “washing down all sacrifices down the drain”. “There can be no greater enmity with the country than not honouring and respecting such sacrifices, not holding them in esteem,” he remarked, highlighting that young soldiers left their homes and families to defend their country. The premier called for an “all-encompassing analysis as to why this happened”, adding that there was “no worse callousness, criminal negligence, and hostility towards the national interest than this”. He said: “All issues of the people were pushed aside — whether it is education, healthcare, or protecting the lives and property of the people — and [having] matters with terrorists instead. I believe that no other example can be found of such hostility against the country, in terms of their attitudes, detachment, and callousness.” PM Shehbaz asserted that 5,000 police vacancies were not filled, Safe City projects were yet to be completed, the capacity of the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) had not been enhanced significantly and neither were special measures taken regarding police training. He recalled that all provinces had agreed at the time of the 2010 National Finance Commission Award that KP, being the front-line region in combatting terrorism, needed ample resources. “From 2010 to today, more than Rs800 billion in funds have either already been provided or are being provided under this,” he stressed. “However, not only did it resurface, but the weapons needed to counter terrorism, the required capacity, and the trained officers needed were nowhere to be found.” While saying he would not go into the details, the prime minister emphasised that he had assured the provincial governments of ex-chief minister Ali Amin Gandapur and of Sohail Afridi of the Centre’s full support in the fight against terrorism. “But nothing was done regarding this,” he regretted, adding that the government could not remain a “silent spectator” when a “party was stooping to such enmity against the country” and the economy and society were being destroyed. “Therefore, on this occasion we made this one last effort,” the premier said, referring to the province’s interim handover to the federal government under governor’s rule. Highlighting the Centre’s efforts to stabilise the economy over the past two and a half years, PM Shehbaz remarked, “It wouldn’t have been possible [without] unprecedented partnership between political and military hierarchy.” He said the federal government could not remain a silent spectator when “terrorists were roaming around dancing in all areas of KP, and were ruling over some areas in the evening, and collecting extortion” at a time when the stabilisation of Pakistan’s economy was being acknowledged globally. The prime minister recalled the breakdown of the Oct 3 talks between the Centre and reiterated that his government was “compelled to make this decision” of imposing governor’s rule. PM Shehbaz remarked that the province was “shattered with wounds due to the circumstances created in the past several years”. He highlighted the poor law and order situation over the past six years, recalling that security forces and law enforcement agencies had made sacrifices to establish peace in KP. The premier said there was corruption of Rs100bn in the clean drinking water of the Cities Improvement Project and Rs37bn in the “infamous looting” in the case about the Kohistan District Accounts Office . He said that “80,000 people were martyred and the [economy] suffered a loss of several hundred billion dollars. Only then, in 2018, was peace completely restored in this country”. Describing the province as “very beautiful”, the premier expressed his hope that the government “work hard day and night and speedily make it progress towards development and prosperity”. “This is the province that is the first extremely strong wall of the homeland,” he noted. Emergency amid security challenges The Centre had imposed emergency and governor’s rule in KP citing the PTI-led provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The decisions were also endorsed by the Parliament last week amid protests by the opposition. Governor Kundi, along with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, had chaired a meeting of the provincial apex committee a day after governor’s rule was imposed. In the meeting, the governor — who is now in charge of running the province — assured Naqvi he would enforce all policies of the federal government and work together with the security forces for peace and prosperity of the province. Kundi asserted that under the new set-up, tackling terrorism would be the priority. Later that day, Kundi, addressing a press conference, called for greater coordination between the Centre and the province, stressing that policies on counterterrorism will “come from Islamabad [..] not Kabul,” in an apparent jibe at the PTI-led KP government, which has been accused of maintaining a “nexus” with terrorist groups by federal ministers. The Centre’s move to impose governor’s rule and emergency in KP also followed a mobilisation drive and protest march by the PTI and in opposition at the Centre, to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. Intense negotiations between the two sides a week before the imposition of governor’s rule had failed to yield any results, with counterterrorism policy being one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their talks. The PTI said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre denied . It also called for reviewing the counterterrorism policy, while the latter criticised the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objected to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban. Soon after, the Centre also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in KP. Federal ministers have also alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, stating that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there. Curbing Criminal Economies in the Amazon Basin mloukili Thu, 10/15/2026 - 14:05 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Commentary / Europe 15 October 2026 12 minutes Curbing Criminal Economies in the Amazon Basin Criminal groups have taken over swathes of the Amazon, fuelling violence and environmental destruction through illicit business. In this excerpt from the EU Watch List 2026 – Autumn Edition , Crisis Group shows how the EU and member states can curb these activities and ecological damage. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Download PDF Full Report Download Full Report Select your download language English Spanish Also available in Español Español English Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy European Union Amazon The Amazon, the world’s largest tropical rainforest, is vital for planetary wellbeing. But it is also the source of several commodities, often obtained and sold illegally, that are in high commercial demand. Expanding markets for gold, wood, beef, critical minerals, wildlife, soy and cocaine, among other licit and illicit goods, have resulted in widespread environmental harm, including deforestation and contamination of soil and waterways . The alarming result is that parts of the Amazon are now releasing more carbon into the atmosphere than they absorb, contributing to global warming. Meanwhile, the crime rings involved in supplying some of these items have tightened their grip on swathes of the Amazon , particularly its rivers and estuaries. The profits they reap allow them to challenge state authority and co-opt officials. They use lethal violence against Indigenous and other residents to consolidate their hold. Europe is a major destination for many of the Amazon’s illicit or illegally produced goods. It is also at the forefront of efforts to contain global climate change, a cause that depends for its success on preserving ecosystems such as the Amazon. Yet European governments have been hesitant to address the intersection of trafficking and organised crime in the Amazon, which makes the job of preserving the rainforest much harder. The EU and its member states should work closely with South American partners to improve security cooperation, harmonise legal norms around environmental crimes, back Indigenous community responses aimed at curtailing illicit businesses and support the creation of legal livelihoods in the Amazon. This set of initiatives could help weaken the criminal groups bringing violence to the Amazon and limit the environmental damage they cause. Aerial view taken during a Greenpeace flyover of illegal mining areas in Kayapo indigenous territory in Para state, Brazil, on 19 March, 2025. AFP / Pablo Porciuncula Organised Crime in the Jungle Over the last decade, criminal groups have extended their reach across the Amazon, both to exploit its natural riches and to use its rivers to carry goods to seaports for shipment to European and Asian buyers. Governments in the Amazon basin have taken action to stop these activities, seeking to curb both the environmental degradation they cause and the attendant violence, but shifting political priorities and lack of resources have meant that the effects of their campaigns have been uneven. Criminals take advantage of discrepancies among the various countries’ penal codes to avoid running afoul of regulations and facing prosecution. For instance, Brazil prohibits the commercial export of many wildlife species, while Guyana and Suriname permit it under a quota. As a result, traffickers can catch animals in Brazil, move them across one of the borders and ship them legally from Guyana and Suriname without needing to forge documents. Shifting Drug Routes Drug traffickers have long taken advantage of the Amazon’s vast expanses and weak state presence to cultivate and process coca crops and transport cocaine, which they then send across the Atlantic Ocean. Despite prohibition measures, South American production of the narcotic is at an all-time high, spurred by a boom in consumption in Europe. In response, Europe has continued to focus its law enforcement efforts on drug interdictions , largely as shipments approach the continent’s ports. The U.S., for its part, has turned to military firepower, launching a wave of attacks on alleged drug-carrying boats along routes across the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean, killing almost 240 suspected traffickers so far. Some reports claim that these U.S. strikes have pushed additional quantities of drugs onto Amazon routes, but more research is needed to verify such a shift. That said, evidence does show that drug markets in the rainforest are more robust than ever: in Brazil alone, there was a 574 per cent increase in cocaine seizures in the country’s nine Amazon basin states between 2019 and 2024. With the state’s reach limited in much of the Amazon, traffickers move cocaine from Bolivia, Colombia and Peru to ports in the Guianas and Brazil. Barcarena, where the Amazon empties into the Atlantic, is among the most important exit points. Source: Crisis Group research; OpenStreetMap / CRISIS GROUP The limited reach of the state in much of the Amazon means that traffickers face few obstacles in transporting cocaine, which is produced mostly in Bolivia, Colombia and Peru, to ports in the Guianas (as the north-eastern part of South America comprising French Guiana, Guyana and Suriname is known) and Brazil, from where they ship it to Europe, either directly or via West Africa . Barcarena, the Brazilian town where the Amazon river system empties into the Atlantic, is among the most important exit points. Cocaine leaves through the Vila do Conde container terminal concealed in legitimate cargo, usually without the exporter’s knowledge. Recent shipments have been found in açaí , quartz and soy meal consignments bound for Portugal, the Netherlands, France and Australia. Crisis Group has previously written about how criminal groups in the region collaborate, with each playing a role in transforming coca into cocaine, moving it through the Amazon and distributing it worldwide. These networks encompass Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho in Brazil; the National Liberation Army or ELN, Comandos de la Frontera and other FARC dissident groups in Colombia; and Los Lobos and Los Choneros in Ecuador. All these organisations have employed violence and payoffs to quash local resistance and rid themselves of state agents who get in the way of doing business. But, reflecting what is happening elsewhere in Latin America, competition among criminal groups in the Amazon is also becoming lethal. Along the Orinoco River and Río Negro, shared by Colombia and Venezuela, a long-time alliance between the ELN and FARC dissidents of the Segunda Marquetalia came to an end in August 2025 , triggering clashes in which the groups used landmines and drones. As rivals jostle for control of markets, violence is likely to get worse. The expansion of organised crime is particularly pernicious for young residents of areas where they operate. These groups often hire children and adolescents to help with logistical tasks, paying them in drugs rather than cash. The kids then sell the drugs, causing substance abuse to rise in riverine villages. Along the Amazon River in Colombia, for example, Indigenous Ticuna people report that drug sale points have cropped up in rural areas. With no harm reduction programs in place, elders worry about the future of their children and the long-term effects on their communities. Gold and Other Commodities Many drug trafficking organisations have diversified into illegal gold mining, as rising prices for the metal have made it lucrative , with sales often raking in more income for criminals than cocaine. Illicit gold extraction can destroy ecosystems, as miners raze forests and pollute rivers and their banks with mercury (used to separate bits of gold from sediment). Mining sites have also been linked to grave human rights abuses, including violence against Indigenous leaders, sexual exploitation and child labour. Besides being highly profitable, gold is appealing because the product itself is easily transported and difficult to trace to its source. Even if illegally extracted, it can be funnelled into the legal supply chain at little risk just by forging paperwork. Criminal organisations seize this opportunity to “clean” drug trafficking proceeds by either investing in illegal gold mining or purchasing gold directly. The Guianas are a hub for these practices, as local regulations allow miners to absorb gold extracted in Venezuela and then re-export it as if it was locally produced. Over the past decade, much of Venezuela’s illicit gold has reached Switzerland and Belgium in this way , with large quantities also transiting Amsterdam. Security forces throughout the Amazon region are also concerned about Venezuela’s growing role in laundering illegal gold from Brazil and Colombia. After Caracas adopted a new mining law and U.S. sanctions authorities provided a licence for sales from the state company Minerven, illicit gold sellers have sought to mix their products into this newly legal pipeline for international sales. Law enforcement officials have told Crisis Group that “dirty gold” from other Amazon countries often passes through European airports for sale to refiners and minerals traders in countries including Germany and Italy. As with drug trafficking, competition over mines frequently results in violence. As with drug trafficking, competition over mines frequently results in violence. The ELN-Segunda Marquetalia fighting, which has spread from Venezuela into Colombia, was sparked by contests over gold and critical mineral mining sites as well as narcotics. In April, for example, these two groups battled in the Venezuelan municipality of Cedeño, displacing dozens of families . Other coveted minerals can also be found in the Amazon, including coltan, tin and tungsten. More than half the world’s critical mineral deposits are located on or in proximity to Indigenous lands. In Brazil, for instance, companies have sought permission to look for critical minerals in or near almost 44 per cent of the country’s Indigenous territories. The people residing in remote areas of the rainforest are often the victims of violence and other abuses committed by armed groups undertaking exploration. In Venezuela’s Amazonas and Bolívar states, coltan, tin and tungsten are mined in Indigenous lands that are under guerrilla control ; residents told Crisis Group that child labour, sexual violence and summary executions are frequent. To make matters worse, Venezuelan state forces in the area are reportedly collecting kickbacks from the groups, rather than protecting the vulnerable, and at times enriching themselves by taking more direct control of mines. Meanwhile, cattle ranching, land grabbing and industrial agriculture, the main drivers of Amazon deforestation, continue to grow as criminal groups launder money by investing in land, livestock and agribusiness. In Brazil, the expansion of agriculture and cattle ranching accounted for 99 per cent of native vegetation loss in 2025. What is at Stake for the EU Europe is tied to the violence and environmental damage done by resource extraction and trafficking in the Amazon because it is a major customer for the commodities in question. At the same time, the EU presents itself as a partner in forest protection and sustainable development as ways to mitigate the effects of climate change. But the attention paid by European leaders to the Amazon crisis has been fitful, due partly to sheer distance and partly to preoccupation with more immediate problems like the Ukraine and Middle East wars. European governments are also inclined to avoid engaging with Latin America in ways that might upset the U.S., particularly under the Trump administration, which has made clear it wants Washington to be the dominant influence in the Western Hemisphere. Even in law enforcement cooperation, which Washington seems to favour, Europe is keen to avoid any initiatives resembling U.S. backing for lethal armed force. The health of the rainforest and its inhabitants, however, is crucial for the EU in several ways. In recognition of its importance to achieving Europe’s climate goals, the EU-funded Amazonia+ program currently supports eight Amazon countries in tackling deforestation, forest degradation and wildfires. Germany and France, meanwhile, have pledged up to 1.5 billion euros combined to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF), a new Brazilian-led fund that pays countries for each hectare of forest they preserve. Furthermore, in March the EU adopted a binding 2040 target of slashing net emissions by 90 per cent from 1990 levels. While at least 85 per cent of that cut must be achieved domestically, up to 5 per cent of the remainder may be met by buying carbon credits from projects outside the EU (each credit will represent one tonne of emissions cut, or carbon removed somewhere else on Europe’s behalf). Cooperating with states and civil society in the Amazon could help meet these objectives. Another issue of acute concern for Europe is critical minerals. The EU and its member states are keen to diversify imports of these minerals , which have important applications in the green, digital, defence and aerospace sectors, and the Amazon is well positioned to form part of its supply chains. At present, Europe relies heavily on China, which builds more than 90 per cent of the world’s rare earth magnets and dominates refining of these elements. The EU’s Critical Raw Materials Act aims to ensure EU access to a secure and sustainable supply of these materials. Of the 34 minerals on the EU’s critical raw materials list , 25 are extracted in Latin America. Brussels has already established partnerships with two Latin American countries, Argentina and Chile , aimed at boosting cooperation on critical raw mineral extraction, while negotiations with Brazil are under way. Brazil already supplies over 80 per cent of the EU’s niobium, with most of its unprocessed copper coming from Brazil, Peru and Chile. Responsible mining investment in Latin America could help European countries acquire these valuable elements while limiting the harmful consequences for local communities and the environment. The EU has already adopted rules to address concerns about criminal profiteering and abuses in the mineral supply chain. But these are restricted in scope, and some have yet to kick in. The EU’s Conflict Minerals Regulation requires importers to carry out due diligence to guarantee their supply chains are not funding armed groups, violence or abuses, though it applies only to tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold, not the full list of critical raw materials. Another initiative, the Critical Raw Materials Act , allows the EU to fast-track certain projects, so long as they put environmental, social and human rights safeguards in place. Yet only a small subset of projects is covered, and there is too little transparency about which ones are chosen and how to ensure compliance. Enforcement of the landmark Deforestation Regulation, meant to bar soy, cattle, timber and other commodities from the EU market unless proven to have no connection to deforestation, has now been pushed back twice under pressure from industry and trade partners. It is now set to enter force in December. As trafficking networks fan out across Europe, drug-related violence has shot up in and around port cities. Arguably, however, European states’ main concern is the cocaine pouring into their cities from South America, including via the Amazon trafficking route. As trafficking networks fan out across Europe, drug-related violence has shot up in and around port cities like Antwerp and Rotterdam, as well as in other hotspots in Italy, Spain, France and Germany. Crisis Group’s conversations with European officials suggest that curbing drug trafficking is a pressing policy concern for many governments and voters. Europe’s efforts to address drug trafficking in Latin America have already touched on the Amazon route, mostly through the now completed COPOLAD program. In Peru, for example, the program funded the creation of an early warning system to flag environmental crimes and criminal threats to human rights defenders. EU cooperation initiatives such as EL PAcCTO 2.0 have also funded projects to boost cross-border law enforcement cooperation on illegal gold mining. In late 2025, EL PAcCTO, Interpol and the Dutch police environmental crime unit aided Brazil, French Guiana, Guyana and Suriname in the first transnational operation to this effect , known as the Guyana Shield, which resulted in 198 arrests and seizures of illicit goods. Germany, for its part, has long funded the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO), while other European countries take part in specific initiatives on security in the region. France, for example, has deployed a liaison officer to the international police cooperation centre in Manaus, Brazil, created following the ACTO’s 2023 Belém Declaration . The EU is also supporting efforts to enhance border management and multinational frontier cooperation as well as to counter human trafficking in Latin America through EUROFRONT , including Amazon-region borders between Colombia and Ecuador. To tackle the challenges facing the Amazon, the EU and its member states should: Help improve law enforcement cooperation and legal harmonisation. The EU and its member states should pair seizures of illicit commodities with asset recovery and money laundering investigations that target the European counterparts of local criminal syndicates. The EU should also step up support for multinational law enforcement and expand port and container security cooperation with Amazon exit points such as Barcarena and the Guianas, where interdiction is weakest and cocaine shipments are on the rise. The EU and its partners should also push for legal harmonisation – eg, of illicit trafficking definitions in various penal codes – within the ACTO and Andean Community. To this end, the EU should support a proposal spearheaded by Brazil to add environmental crimes to the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime. Strengthen legislation governing gold and critical minerals markets. Critical raw materials refined outside the EU and imported as finished components fall outside the EU’s regulatory frameworks on conflict minerals and deforestation, while unrefined rare earths and bauxite are not covered at all. To ensure that its imports are not linked to criminal activity, the EU, its member states and its partners should support efforts such as those led by Brazil’s Federal Police and Colombia’s geological service to build gold and/or critical mineral traceability systems. The EU should also support law enforcement efforts targeting secondary products used in illicit mining, such as mercury, fuel, cyanide, explosives and mining equipment. Design a holistic approach toward the Amazon. The withdrawal of U.S. development aid has left gaps in environmental support and programming for alternative livelihoods in communities across the Amazon. While Europe cannot completely fill those spaces, the EU should focus support on market access, education and climate adaptation, particularly in coca-growing and gold-mining regions. Global Gateway – the EU’s strategy for financing infrastructure and connectivity projects in partner countries – should channel private investment toward sustainable infrastructure that could help make legal activities such as small-scale farming and fishing more commercially feasible, reducing the incentives for local communities to participate in illicit activity. Simultaneously, to slow deforestation, the EU should double down on results-based strategies such as that of the TFFF, which offers direct benefits to states that succeed in conserving forested areas. Back Indigenous governance. The EU and its member states should encourage capitals across the region to work closely with Indigenous organisations in monitoring illegal activities in remote jungles, since they are well placed to spot criminal activity where state security institutions are weak or absent.
