Israel’s Elections: What’s at Stake? eschelhaas Thu, 10/15/2026 - 18:12 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List A Palestinian farmer walks past election banners near the Palestinian-owned olive groves in the village of Rantes near Ramallah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on October 6, 2026. ZAIN JAAFAR / AFP Q&A / Middle East & North Africa 15 October 2026 16 minutes Israel’s Elections: What’s at Stake? Israelis will soon head to the polls for the first time since the 7 October 2023 attacks and the seismic events that followed. In this Q&A, Crisis Group experts look at what issues concern the voters and what change the balloting may bring. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Related Tags Israel/Palestine What is happening? On 27 October, Israelis will head to the polls at a particularly fraught moment in the country’s history. The vote is the first since the deadly Hamas assault of 7 October 2023, which killed 1,318 Israelis and precipitated seismic events in Israel-Palestine and across the Middle East – not least Israel’s destruction of Gaza and killing of at least 74,000 of its people. The repercussions of this turmoil for Israeli electoral politics now wait to be seen. With Israel still entangled in several conflicts – including in the Palestinian territories, in Lebanon, in Syria and with Iran – and at the centre of increasingly passionate domestic political debates around the world, Israelis, Palestinians and millions of others will be watching closely. About a dozen political parties are expected to cross the proportional threshold (3.25 per cent of the national vote) needed to enter the parliament, or Knesset, which has 120 seats. Two main blocs – of nearly equal weight, according to polls – are facing off against each other. One is an alliance of hard-right parties dominated by Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister and head of the Likud Party. The other camp is led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of Yashar (meaning “straight”, as in honest), a centre-right party he founded in 2025. A third group, made up of parties that represent Israel’s Palestinian Arab minority, is projected to capture a smaller but critical share of seats. Defining party platforms is an inexact science. The vertical axis reflects domestic issues; the horizontal, external ones (including occupied territories). Box size reflects poll projections of seat numbers. Sources: israel-polls-2026.pages.dev. Party positions are Crisis Group assessments, building on Peter Lintl’s framework for Israel’s 2022 election, “Israel’s Anti-liberal Coalition”, Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik, 27 January 2023 / CRISIS GROUP Notwithstanding nuances among the various parties, the 2026 contest is largely a battle between different right-wing approaches to governing an Israel that has all but consolidated its control of the Palestinian territories – ie, the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem. Questions that outsiders might expect to be at the centre of election debates, such as Israel’s almost 70-year occupation of these lands, preoccupy Israeli voters far less than internal issues, including the rule of law and relations between religion and state. That divergence raises complex questions about what change the world can expect to see after 27 October – and what is likely to stay the same. What are the chances of Netanyahu remaining in power? Significant, but it is too close to call. On one hand, the election comes at an especially tough time for Netanyahu. Poll numbers measuring his personal popularity and the degree of public trust he enjoys have been low for most of the period since 7 October 2023. His many years of domineering leadership – and in the view of former coalition partners, his corruption, manipulations and betrayals – have shrunk his pool of potential political allies. His Likud Party, the dominant force on the Israeli right since the 1970s, now polls lower than Eisenkot’s Yashar. Polls also show that given a choice between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, Israelis tend to favour the former general (who also garnered public sympathy after his son was killed in action in Gaza), over the sitting prime minister. For months, the parties that make up Netanyahu’s current coalition have together consistently polled well below the numbers needed for a 61-seat majority. A new hard-right party, Amcha Yisrael, led by former general Ofer Winter, could also be a handicap for Likud: it could draw votes away from Netanyahu’s party, but it could also “burn” votes, meaning render them irrelevant, since votes for smaller parties are discounted from the tally if they fail to cross the 3.25 per cent threshold. Yet Netanyahu, who turns 77 on 21 October, has long defied presumptions that his career has run its course. His skill at juggling crises is legendary; the latest ones include a lengthy trial for alleged corruption , widespread anger at his gradual overhaul of the judiciary, charges of failing to heed warnings ahead of the 2023 Hamas attack and then shirking responsibility for it, Israel’s sinking international reputation and an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court, not to mention an open-ended, seven-front war spanning the Middle East. Some of his opponents, recalling what he has done in past election campaigns, worry that the pugnacious prime minister may resort to tactics aimed at dividing his opponents. In particular, they fear he may try to discourage or intimidate would-be voters among Israel’s Palestinian Arab citizens. Some are also apprehensive that, should he become desperate, Netanyahu might launch a new military action, perhaps against Iran, in an attempt to postpone the election . Regardless of any such manoeuvres, the far-right, religious, pro-settler coalition led by the prime minister is strong. It has survived four turbulent years in power and still enjoys a firm base of support, including among young and first-time voters. True, the Netanyahu bloc has consistently polled well below a majority needed to form a coalition, and the anti-Netanyahu bloc – a disparate collection of right-wing, centrist and centre-left Jewish parties, as well as two lists of Palestinian Arab parties – represents a bigger proportion of the electorate in raw numbers. But several of the latter camp’s Jewish leaders have publicly sworn they would not form a government with the Arab parties, implying they might even be loath to rely on these parties’ Knesset votes to bolster a minority coalition. With neither bloc able to reach a majority alone, the Arab parties look like kingmakers. But they will not join a Netanyahu-led coalition, and the anti-Netanyahu bloc is wary of inviting them into government. Source: Crisis Group estimates based on aggregate polling data up to 14 October. Some votes may be “lost” to parties that fail to reach the 3.25 per cent threshold. / CRISIS GROUP This reluctance to share power with Arabs is not new, but it has become a matter of political consensus since 7 October 2023. The Netanyahu camp’s repeated claim that its adversaries can only win by joining ranks with Arab parties is also a sign of how the far right now shapes the political climate: it appeals to anti-Arab prejudice to alarm voters and taunt opponents, as well as to trap them into possibly self-defeating commitments. The delegitimisation of any coalition that might include Arabs has increased Netanyahu’s chances of remaining as caretaker prime minister until another round of elections a few months later, not by winning, but by blocking the other side. What are the most important – and divisive – issues for Israeli voters? The elections are in part a referendum on Netanyahu, particularly on his responsibility (or lack thereof) for the 7 October 2023 events and his actions thereafter. Many Israelis blame him for a policy of accommodating Hamas’s rule in Gaza in the years leading up to the lethal attack, including the facilitation of Qatari financing; for reportedly ignoring warnings of an impending Hamas operation; for allegedly relegating Israeli hostages to the back burner among war priorities in Gaza; and for refusing to name an independent commission of inquiry into the intelligence and other failures that helped make the Hamas assault so deadly. Netanyahu’s supporters dismiss such charges as a political inquisition led by Israel’s “deep state” (which they allege includes judges and generals) along with left-leaning media and foreign-funded organisations. They defend the prime minister’s wars, arguing that he has smashed Hamas in Gaza and Hizbollah in Lebanon and (having persuaded the U.S. to join in) severely weakened the Islamic Republic of Iran, securing Israel’s uncontested regional primacy. The legacy of Netanyahu’s coalition, widely viewed as the most extreme in Israel’s history, is also at stake in that referendum. Since taking office in December 2022, the right-wing Likud and its harder-right partners have pursued an aggressive agenda of redesigning parts of the Israeli state, the occupation of the Palestinian territories and Israel’s regional surroundings. They have sought to weaken the judicial system as an institutional check (indeed the only remaining one) on the executive and legislature, at the same time as working to entrench government influence over Israeli media, tighten restrictions on civil society, extend religious laws and practices into various spheres of public life, and accelerate Israel’s de facto annexation of the West Bank. Meanwhile, they also stand accused of failing to support Jewish border towns affected by years of war, such as those near the Lebanese frontier, whose residents fled Hizbollah rocket fire and still consider it unsafe to return. Many Israelis who regard themselves as secular, socially liberal and advocates of mamlakhtiyut (meaning the primacy of the state over factional interests) view the government’s ambitions for extending its power as anathema. These critics accuse firebrand leaders such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir of endangering Israel’s democracy, its social cohesion and its image abroad. A fresh government unbeholden to the far right, they say, could help repair some of that damage. A dispute that encapsulates these multiple fissures concerns the conscription of Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) citizens into the Israeli army. Even as the Haredims’ share of Israel’s population grew from under 5 per cent in 1980 to nearly 15 per cent today, they continued to enjoy exemption from state service on religious grounds until 2024, when the Supreme Court overruled the exception. Two Haredi parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, which were formally part of Netanyahu’s coalition until mid-2025, sought to circumvent the ruling via new legislation that the prime minister promised to push. But they failed to reach an agreement that would pass the Knesset, as some members of the ruling coalition – including within Likud – favour universal conscription. In practice, most Haredi youths continue to dodge the draft. Opposition leaders ... dismiss partnering with Haredi parties unless they agree that their constituents should submit to the draft. The Haredim are deeply unpopular with many political factions. Opposition leaders, many of whom are secular or of military background, dismiss partnering with Haredi parties unless they agree that their constituents should submit to the draft. Pressure to enforce the law has mounted from exhausted army reservists whose lives have been disrupted by repeated call-ups over the last three years. The military has also repeatedly warned that it faces a personnel shortage, especially in light of the government’s demand that soldiers protect increasing numbers of settler outposts in the West Bank. For the 20 per cent of Israel’s citizenry who are Palestinian, the top issues are different. Many see blocking the far right as vital to protecting their precarious civil rights and to ensuring greater access to state resources, as well as to mitigating Israel’s worsening policies in the occupied territories. But most Arab voters also have a particularly urgent concern: restoring their personal safety amid an alarming surge in organised crime and gun violence in Arab towns, which has reached record levels under the watch of Ben-Gvir’s national security ministry and the police it oversees. The two Arab-led slates, the Joint List (made up of Hadash, which identifies as an Arab-Jewish socialist party; Ta’al, which describes itself as an Arab movement for renewal; and Balad, a Palestinian Arab nationalist party) and the Islamist Ra’am, in theory have the potential to become “kingmakers”. Neither the pro- nor anti-Netanyahu blocs will be able to reach a parliamentary majority without Arab support, either as part of a governing coalition or as outside votes to back a given coalition. But it is unclear how and to what extent such electoral clout can translate into collective gains when even most of Israel’s mainstream opposition reject partnering with them. The Arab parties themselves are not in lockstep; while Ra’am is seeking to join a coalition with only domestic concerns in mind, the Joint List stipulated that at least some demands relating to the occupied territories, such as a diplomatic pathway to a Palestinian state, must also be addressed in order for it to provide a “safety net” (ie, serve as external support) for a minority government. Is the conflict with the Palestinians playing a role in the elections? For the ruling parties, yes; for the opposition, barely. In addition to its war on Gaza, the Netanyahu government has spent its tenure hastening Israel’s de facto annexation of the West Bank and extending “Jewish sovereignty” through settlements, making the prevention of a Palestinian state its flagship goal. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a portfolio in the defence ministry, in particular has spearheaded efforts to advance de jure annexation. The Likud is promoting the slogan “Yamin o’ Falastin” (Hebrew for “ The Right or Palestine ”) to suggest that any alternative government would pave the way for Palestinian statehood, notably because it would depend on support from the Arab parties. Leading coalition figures loudly applaud the devastation of Gaza, with some others still promoting the expulsion of its people and the re-establishment of Jewish settlements in the strip. Opposition Jewish figures are less coherent or vocal on the topic, but by and large they do not call the settlement enterprise’s continuation into question. Some blast the government’s support for the more extremist settler agendas; virtually none supports Palestinian statehood, at least not in the near future; and many try to ignore the Palestinian question altogether. One possible exception is Avigdor Lieberman, a former defence minister and leader of the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu, a party that largely represents Russian immigrants, and who proposes that Jordan assume responsibility for ruling Palestinians inside a truncated portion of the territory. The centre-left Democrats, led by reserve major general and parliamentarian Yair Golan, is perhaps the only Jewish party that openly supports a two-state solution, yet it conditions a Palestinian state on a host of caveats (such as maintaining long-term Israeli security control of the entire territory) and argues that in any case the time is not right for such a state to emerge. Only the two Arab lists consistently promote Palestinian rights and self-determination, though Ra’am largely relegates these issues to secondary importance in its campaign. One West Bank issue that has generated Israeli debate is mounting settler violence against Palestinians. One West Bank issue that has generated Israeli debate is mounting settler violence against Palestinians, with even Netanyahu condemning what he insists are “fringe groups”. What appears to concern Israel’s mainstream media and Jewish voters, however, is less the harm being done to Palestinians than the added burden being placed on Israel’s occupying army and the state’s resources. Many also lament the further blemishes on Israel’s international image. Next to nothing has been done to stop the attacks in practice, and official policies that more broadly immiserate West Bank Palestinians, such as economic strangulation , home demolitions and land expropriation, rarely elicit comment from the (non-Arab) opposition. In a late August interview, Eisenkot said the army had “lost its control” of the West Bank due to the Netanyahu government’s policies and its emboldening of settler vigilantes. He also criticised the push to build the controversial E1 settlement , which would split the West Bank in two, as a “mistake” that has angered Israel’s allies. In a more recent interview , he claimed that a Yashar-led government would not only curb the actions of what he has called “Jewish terrorists” but also evacuate all outposts considered illegal under Israeli law in the West Bank (under international law, all settlements on occupied territory are considered illegal). It is fair to assume that he might also freeze construction of E1. But Eisenkot has also described the two-state solution as “delusional” and stressed that “I very much believe in settlement in Judea and Samaria” (the biblical term that many Israelis use for the West Bank). Naftali Bennett – head of the Together slate, a former prime minister and past head of the Yesha settler council – is unapologetic about his support for annexing the West Bank’s Area C (ie, the part that the 1993-1995 Oslo accords left under full Israeli administrative and security control) and his rejection of Palestinian statehood. The same is true of opposition figure Lieberman, as well as two other prominent politicians, Benny Gantz and Yoaz Hendel, who have positioned themselves as unaligned with either bloc. The competing parties may differ over whether to prop up the Palestinian Authority with financial and security cooperation and who should govern Gaza, but these are peripheral rather than central disagreements. Vis-á-vis the Palestinians, the next Israeli government will assume power on a markedly different footing from when the current one was elected four years ago. In the interval, Israel has swallowed more territory and squeezed Palestinians into smaller cantons in both Gaza and the West Bank. It has razed cities and refugee camps and emboldened a settler movement that will likely remain feverishly active regardless of who is in power. There is now near-consensus among Israeli Jews about maintaining security control throughout the occupied territories – from the proverbial river to the sea. But while the far right wants to turbo-charge the settlement enterprise and turn up the heat on the Palestinians further, many Israelis would prefer to bracket the issue, reverting to policies that can manage the conflict on their terms rather than seeking a political agreement with the Palestinians. The latter approach kept the occupation out of sight and out of mind – but also kept its end out of reach. Such shades of difference could change the level of physical and economic violence meted out to Palestinians, which is no small matter. But they would barely touch the core of the occupation itself. Have Israel’s other military campaigns in the region – in Lebanon, Syria and Iran – influenced the domestic political scene? Surprisingly little. A majority of Jewish Israelis has consistently supported Israel’s wars, with tens of thousands of soldiers and reservists continuing to serve despite widespread disillusionment with Netanyahu’s government. Even when Israelis were forced into shelters for weeks on end during the present war with Iran, public support remained high. In many ways, the seven-front war of the past three years has simply accelerated Israel’s rightward shift. Such criticism as there is tends to demand a harder, not softer approach. The centrist opposition leader Yair Lapid, whose Yesh Atid party is running alongside Bennett on the Together slate, said Israel should not have stopped at assassinating Iran’s leadership but should have bombed its oil and gas facilities during the second phase of the war, which started in late February. Bennett, for his part, has made classifying Qatar as an enemy state a central talking point. In November 2024, days before a ceasefire was brokered between Lebanon and Israel, Gantz, an ostensibly centre-right former general, called on the military to bomb Lebanese government assets. What are the most likely outcomes? Barring a dramatic development, and assuming the most credible polls are largely correct, four plausible scenarios could emerge after election day: A hung parliament. Neither bloc wins a decisive parliamentary majority or ropes enough parties into supporting a minority government. This outcome is possible, for instance, if Eisenkot or his allies refuse to bring the Arab lists into the fold or to rely on their outside support. The result would be another round of elections. In this case, Netanyahu would stay on as caretaker prime minister, with his sitting coalition continuing to hold the reins of government for several months, pending a fresh vote. Yashar edges out Likud and forms a government drawn from the opposition. This scenario would likely require Eisenkot to partner in some fashion with the two lists that represent Palestinian citizens – perhaps as external backers, instead of coalition partners – with the principal aim of keeping Netanyahu and his bloc out of power. There is precedent for this arrangement (albeit in starkly different circumstances), such as when Arab parties gave outside support to Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin from 1992 until his assassination in 1995. But shifts in public opinion, especially after the 7 October 2023 attacks, make reliance on the Joint List in particular a politically fraught proposition. Parties or politicians break ranks. Following an inconclusive result, Eisenkot or Netanyahu could convince parties or individual Knesset members in the opposing bloc to defect and form a “national unity government”. There could be several permutations along these lines. For example, commentators have suggested that the opposition consider forming a government with Likud, excluding far-right parties such as Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit. Netanyahu himself has floated this possibility. Though it got broadly negative responses, there is recent precedent, albeit with mixed results. In 2020, Netanyahu persuaded Gantz, then his biggest rival, to join a coalition, causing Gantz’s Blue and White Party to split. The government dissolved only a few months later. A bloc defies the polls and clinches a parliamentary majority. This outcome is highly unlikely. It would mean that months of polls have been egregiously wrong, given that all have said neither bloc is close to winning 61 seats. A surprise could conceivably occur if several parties fail to cross the electoral threshold, thus “burning” a large share of votes, or if turnout for certain parties far exceeds expectations. Israel’s electoral system has always been prone to twists and turns, but the 2026 election’s result is arguably less predictable than usual. Dry numbers from various sources provide hints. An independent aggregator of opinion polls over recent months suggests that the chances of either bloc achieving an outright majority are well under 10 per cent. Online betting sites , which are a rough indicator of where investors put their money, give Eisenkot and Yashar slightly greater respective odds of becoming the next prime minister and largest party in the Knesset. Still, even in that scenario Eisenkot would have to decide whether to partner with Arab parties, a question he has skirted until now. The outcome may not be all that stable. Despite a reshuffling of parties and emergence of new personalities, and though the political spectrum as a whole has shifted further rightward, Israeli voters appear to be caught in the same deadlock that has largely held since 2019 – one that led Israeli voters to go to the voting booths five times in three years until the current government took office – and held onto it for four years. The recent uptick in international pressure on Israel’s West Bank policies – notably, the UK-led settlement trade ban in September – is unlikely to fundamentally shift Israeli views in the near term, though it may affect voter turnout for one side or the other. Many Israelis are distrustful or dismissive of foreign criticism, believing that outsiders do not understand their nation’s unique circumstances, are overly fixated on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict or harbour anti-Israeli or anti-Semitic views. That said, they are not oblivious to the threat of isolation. They know that Israel’s brutal Gaza war, its increasingly aggressive policies in the West Bank and the proliferation of Middle East conflicts have all come at a high reputational cost to Israel, not only harming its diplomatic standing but also affecting its citizens’ interactions with the outside world. The question is whether mounting outside pressure can constructively shift Israeli calculations on war and peace after election day – regardless of the coalition that emerges. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 10/16/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 16 October 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 16 October 2026 IRAN Iranian attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have surged in October to date, with more than two dozen vessels struck since the month began. Meanwhile, Washington is maintaining its blockade of Iranian ports while backing oil shipments along the Omani coast, where smaller tankers transfer cargo to larger vessels outside the strait. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick in Iranian strikes is an effort to counter a rebound in oil flows that showed Tehran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz was weakening. Iran wants Washington to accept its proposed terms for a ceasefire that reopens the waterway in exchange for sanctions relief and an end to the U.S. blockade. But a diplomatic breakthrough appears less likely than the two sides setting off another escalatory spiral. SUDAN The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a UN-backed hunger monitor, warned Monday of growing famine risks in Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan regions, driven by conflict, displacement and inadequate aid funding, and compounded by an El Niño-induced drought. This news comes as Sudan’s army reports advances against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in parts of North Kordofan and West Darfur. Meanwhile, the RSF continues to mount attacks in Blue Nile and to target El Obeid in North Kordofan with drones. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says the army’s gains could make it more confident of victory, while continued RSF offensives suggest that this group, too, sees opportunities for battlefield gains. The continued fighting is likely to further complicate diplomatic efforts to end the war and ease Sudan’s humanitarian crisis. UKRAINE This past Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, saying each had agreed to halt attacks on the other’s energy infrastructure, following a deal he made to buy Russian diesel and ease related U.S. sanctions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he learned of the ceasefire through social media, adding that Washington threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stopped striking Russian refineries. Ukrainian forces also reported restrictions on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service, which they depend on for communications and drone operations. Washington says it continues to share intelligence with Ukraine. Zelenskyy this week announced the resumption of refinery attacks as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued unabated. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says any disruption to intelligence or communications would compound Ukraine’s difficulties in protecting its cities and power grid as winter approaches, leaving civilians more vulnerable to prolonged heating and electricity outages. 9 October 2026 HAITI Haiti’s electoral council announced changes to the country’s voting rules Tuesday. The new law, which will likely result in delays to polls presently scheduled for 13 December, will remove provisions that would have disqualified individuals subject to bilateral sanctions imposed by third countries from running for office. SUDAN UN agencies issued statements Tuesday protesting a “sharp increase” in drone warfare that is taking a mounting civilian toll. At least 70 people were killed the previous day when drones hit a hospital in East Darfur. Patients, doctors and nurses were among the dead. Another 28 civilians were killed in drone strikes in North Darfur and North Kordofan Thursday. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says both main belligerents in Sudan’s war, the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), have stepped up their use of drones in an attempt to get an edge on the battlefield. Meanwhile, the risk of spillover into neighbouring countries is heightening, with the RSF taking a town on the Ethiopian border and fighting continuing on the Chadian frontier. 20 March 2026 CHAD - SUDAN A drone attack Wednesday killed seventeen people in Chad’s border town of Tine, including mourners gathered for a funeral and children playing nearby. The Chadian government accused the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan of launching the drone. In late February, the RSF had hit Chadian army positions in Tine, killing several Chadian soldiers. President Mahamat Déby ordered a total closure of the border with Sudan, which could have negative humanitarian consequences. The border has officially been closed since April 2023, but until now authorities have been allowing some refugees and aid shipments through. He also warned that Chad would retaliate for any further strikes on its territory, no matter who is responsible. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says Chad, which hosts around one million Sudanese refugees, increasingly risks getting drawn into the war in Sudan as fighting routinely spills across the border. IRAN Oil and gas prices soared and stock markets dived Thursday after Iran struck Qatar’s main natural gas facility, Ras Laffan. The Iranian attack came a day after Israel hit Iran’s South Pars gas field, one of the world’s largest. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these tit-for-tat attacks on hydrocarbon infrastructure signal a new phase in the conflict, now entering its fourth week, as a global energy crisis looms and Gulf Arab states are increasingly caught in the crossfire, with Saudi Arabia warning of military action against Iran as these states’ patience wears thin. NIGERIA Multiple suicide bombings Monday killed at least 26 people and injured over a hundred in Maiduguri, capital of Nigeria’s Borno state. The bombings come amid a surge of violence in the country’s north east, with both Boko Haram and the Islamic State-West Africa Province, an ISIS affiliate, launching lethal raids. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says the latest attacks indicate that these insurgencies may again be gaining momentum. The M23 rebels who hold the city blamed the Congolese government for the attacks. Kinshasa said an investigation is under way. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says Kinshasa, which has purchased Chinese and Turkish drones, is determined to use its new arsenal to show the rebels they are not safe in their bastions. But with civilian casualties mounting, the government’s growing reliance on drones could backfire by costing it international support. IRAN Amid a widening Middle East conflict sparked by U.S.-Israeli strikes that began two weeks ago, the Islamic Republic effected only the second transition in its most senior post since the 1979 revolution that brought it to power. Mojtaba Khamenei has taken up the position of Supreme Leader, which his father Ali held from 1989 until his death on 28 February in the war’s opening salvo. The first official statement attributed to the younger Khamenei was defiant in tone, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, highlighting the Iranian regime's desire to project continuity under duress, vis-à-vis both its foreign adversaries and its domestic opponents. Many Iranians, meanwhile, are despairing at a leadership transition that so far promises more of the same. LEBANON Israel’s latest military escalation in Lebanon continued to wreak havoc this week. It has also sent more troops into southern Lebanon, with a view to establishing what it calls a “security zone” there. While Israel retains military superiority over Hizbollah, the Shiite party-cum-militia has put up a fight. On Wednesday, it launched a barrage of 100 rockets across the border, which triggered an especially brutal sequence of Israeli air raids. Crisis Group expert David Wood says neither of the belligerents appears ready to stop, even as Lebanese leaders scramble to find a diplomatic off-ramp. In retaliation, Iran fired missiles and drones at Israel, as well as U.S. bases and commercial infrastructure in Gulf states. The conflict's reverberations have quickly spread from the Indian Ocean to the eastern Mediterranean. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Tehran looks prepared for a drawn-out confrontation, betting that it can steadily raise the psychological and economic costs to its adversaries, while maintaining cohesion at the top of the political system despite Khamenei’s demise. Airstrikes can substantially degrade Iran's military capabilities but are unlikely to dislodge the regime, and even if they did, state collapse in Iran would risk unleashing far wider regional disorder. AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Border clashes continued this week after Pakistan declared “open war” with Afghanistan last Friday. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says a drawn-out conflict serves neither side's interests. Outside actors should press Islamabad and Kabul to de-escalate. ECUADOR The U.S. Southern Command said Tuesday Ecuadorian and U.S. forces had begun operations to curb organised crime in Ecuador. They first went after the Colombian armed group Comandos de la Frontera, which is active along the Colombian border. Ecuador’s military says the operations will continue indefinitely. While details are classified, news reports indicate that the U.S. played an advisory role, without putting troops on the ground. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says such cooperation is not new, but the latest announcement signals deeper U.S. involvement. Security ties have deepened as President Daniel Noboa aligns with the Trump administration’s preference for using military force to combat drug trafficking. 27 February 2026 CHAD - SUDAN Chadian authorities Monday announced the immediate closure of the country’s border with Sudan. Chad said the border would remain closed until further notice, while allowing humanitarian exemptions, including for refugees and returnees, as well as approved aid deliveries. Crisis Group expert Charles Bouëssel says N’Djamena should maintain vital cross-border aid and preserve trade that sustains displaced populations. CUBA Cuban authorities Wednesday accused ten people on a U.S.-registered speedboat carrying weapons and tactical gear of attempting infiltration of Cuban territory with “terrorist intentions”. Border guards shot four people dead and wounded six others aboard the boat after its occupants allegedly opened fire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. SYRIA ISIS released an audio statement last weekend denouncing Syria’s interim government and calling for a renewed campaign against its forces. The jihadist group has since claimed responsibility for several attacks on Syrian army personnel in the northern and north-eastern parts of the country. These developments follow last month’s reported mass escape from the al-Hol camp, which held over 20,000 detainees, many of them relatives of suspected ISIS fighters. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis raises the risks associated with pregnancy, the report finds, though health services in conflict-affected places are generally already scarce. Some countries, such as Colombia and Ethiopia, have made progress in reducing maternal mortality through partnerships with NGOs with expertise in service provision in remote areas. But now aid cuts have put such programs in jeopardy, says Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing, even as women are dying in childbirth at alarming rates. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. How War is Reshaping Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” eschelhaas Fri, 10/16/2026 - 18:13 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Iranians commute past a billboard depicting slain Lebanese Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah and Iran's slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Tehran on September 27, 2026. ATTA KENARE / AFP Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 16 October 2026 12 minutes How War is Reshaping Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” Three years of hostilities have transformed Tehran’s network of allies in the Middle East. The Islamic Republic is now relying more heavily on itself, while adapting its relationships with partners whose diminished military utility has not necessarily reduced its commitment to their protection. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Hamidreza Azizi Senior Analyst, Iran https://x.com/HamidRezaAz Related Tags Iran Israel/Palestine Lebanon Syria Developments since 7 October 2023, when Hamas staged its deadly attacks on southern Israel, have transformed Iran’s network of state and non-state allies in the Middle East, as well as their role in Tehran’s military planning and deterrence posture. The weakening of Hamas and Hizbollah at Israel’s hands in the last three years, the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria in December 2024 and, above all, the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran launched in February have altered the vectors of Iranian influence. Together, these events have exposed the limits of an Iranian strategy that had relied chiefly on regional partners to deter adversaries and keep any armed confrontation away from Iran itself. Instead, Tehran now places greater weight on capabilities under its direct control: missiles, drones and the ability to obstruct traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. This evolution does not mean that the “ axis of resistance ”, as Iran calls its collection of allies, has lost all relevance. Rather, it means that axis members are now assuming different functions and that Tehran is approaching them differently. Yemen’s Houthis have gained particularly significant strategic value for Iran because their ability to threaten Red Sea shipping complements Tehran’s leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf. In Iraq, major Shiite factions also remain important political partners, even as Tehran increasingly turns to smaller armed groups to conduct military operations. Overall, the result is a more fragmented network in which heightened local autonomy among Iran’s non-state partners coexists with tighter Iranian control of select cells and smaller armed organisations. Nor is a weaker “axis of resistance” necessarily synonymous with diminished Iranian commitment to its partners. Hizbollah’s lesser contribution to Iranian deterrence, for example, has not reduced Tehran’s determination to protect the Lebanese Shiite movement. To the contrary, Iran has shown itself more willing to use force in Hizbollah’s defence; it also has conditioned reaching a deal terminating its hostilities with the United States on an end to Israel’s campaign in Lebanon. In other terms, Iran still may be drawn into conflicts on its regional partners’ behalf, even as they have become less capable of shielding it from attack. From the Levant to Maritime Chokepoints Prior to October 2023, Iran’s Middle East strategy centred on the Levant . Syria under Assad’s rule was the linchpin, the only Arab state allied with Iran, which provided it with substantial benefits: a land corridor linking Iran and its Iraqi Shiite partners to Hizbollah; proximity to Israel’s borders; and a logistical hub that enabled Tehran to project its influence to the eastern Mediterranean seaboard. In June 2024, Yahya Rahim Safavi , a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps who was then military adviser to Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, likened Iran’s reach through the axis to that of the ancient Persian empire under Cyrus and Xerxes. The advantages of alliance with Assad explain why, over a decade of civil war in Syria, Tehran defended his regime at significant cost. Hizbollah fighters also helped the regime a great deal, battling both its domestic opponents and ISIS. Hizbollah was useful in another important way, offering Tehran a means of threatening Israel from adjacent territory, thus ostensibly deterring it from direct strikes on Iran itself. If Assad’s Syria was a linchpin of the Islamic Republic’s Middle East strategy, the Shiite movement in Lebanon was a principal engine. [Assad’s fall] deprived Iran of its sole Arab state partner and disrupted its supply line to Hizbollah. This arrangement has suffered severe damage since October 2023 , when Hamas – apparently taking even Iran’s leadership by surprise – attacked Israel. The Gaza campaign that Israel launched in response dealt the axis a first blow, although Iran’s relationship with the Palestinian group has never been on par with those it has enjoyed with its other affiliates. Assad’s fall – indirectly part of the chain of events triggered by the Hamas attacks – was far more consequential. It deprived Iran of its sole Arab state partner and disrupted its supply line to Hizbollah. After Hizbollah entered the post-2023 fray, Israeli counter-attacks also inflicted substantial losses on the Lebanese movement’s leadership and military assets, while causing significant death, destruction and displacement in the country. As a result, other Lebanese factions began issuing more urgent calls on Hizbollah to disarm. The setbacks reinforced one another: rebuilding a degraded Hizbollah was a far more daunting task without the Syrian channel that had previously sustained it. These losses notwithstanding, Tehran has yet to forsake the Levant. Hizbollah still has a strong, institutionalised relationship with Iran, significant political weight in Lebanon and the capacity to regroup, at least in part. The Israeli incursions into southern Syria following the Assad regime’s demise may also have benefits for Iran. The Islamic Republic may be banking on local resistance to Israel eventually creating openings for renewed Iranian influence in Syria, though this prospect remains uncertain. For now, Iran has turned its attention to an arena closer to its borders where it retains heftier clout. On 8 June, Esmail Qaani , commander ofthe Revolutionary Guards’ overseas operations arm, the Qods Force, described an emerging “security belt” stretching from the Gulf to the Red Sea. When compared to Safavi’s formulation two years prior, the phrase captures a shift in emphasis from the Levant to the maritime routes linking the Gulf to the western Indian Ocean, a theatre in which Iran’s sway comes more directly from its own place on the map. The Islamic Republic requires neither an allied state nor a non-state partner to project power in the Strait of Hormuz; it can station missiles and drones nearby or even deep inland to threaten naval or commercial vessels in these waters. Tehran’s influence over maritime routes upon which states near and far depend for trade in oil, gas and other vital commodities is boosted by its partnership with the Houthis, who can fire at ships passing in either direction through the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab. Though it no longer serves as a land bridge for arms transfers to Syria and Lebanon, Iraq nonetheless plays an important part in this changing landscape. In particular, it is a locus for coordination between the Houthis and Iraqi armed groups , as well as between the Qods Force and Iraqi groups that have conducted attacks on Gulf Arab states. A More Fragmented Network The shift in Iran’s primary focus from the Levant to the seas has gone hand in hand with organisational changes. Under its late commander Qassem Soleimani, the Qods Force was the principal coordinator of “axis of resistance” activities. Since the U.S. killed Soleimani in January 2020, the Qods Force has not played the same role. Subsequent wars and leadership losses, both within the Revolutionary Guards and among its partners, further discombobulated command structures and impaired joint military operations. As a result, Iran has had to adapt its relationships with groups whose military capabilities and domestic constraints themselves have changed. It has increasingly been compelled to work through smaller groups or selected elements of established organisations. This trend has been most evident in Iraq. As the years passed after Saddam Hussein’s ouster, older Shiite political movements acquired key government positions and economic interests, thus becoming more beholden to popular constituencies. As a result, they are now more hesitant to engage in military action that risks provoking retaliation or eroding their standing. This reluctance was apparent early in the present U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, when several major Iraqi Shiite armed groups declined to mobilise on Tehran’s behalf. Iran had to rely on smaller, less prominent ones – drawn from the self-styled Islamic Resistance in Iraq – to come to its aid. Iraqi sources speak of a network of clandestine cells established by the Revolutionary Guards and operating outside established militias’ command structures that reportedly has been responsible for attacks on Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. These nimbler, smaller groups offer Tehran several advantages. They require fewer resources, they can conceal their affiliations and they can ignore the political constraints holding back their larger counterparts. Their greater ideological cohesion also arguably makes them easier for Tehran to direct. More institutionalised Iraqi Shiite groups remain important to Tehran, notwithstanding their reticence regarding military action in Iran’s defence. But their role has shifted: they are useful principally because they help Iran preserve influence in the country as well as the political space in which smaller armed groups are free to operate. Iran’s changing relationship with Hizbollah illustrates another type of adjustment to similar pressures. Though the movement retains a substantial organisation that helps Tehran sustain influence in Lebanon, Hizbollah’s military actions increasingly resemble those of a guerrilla group – quick-hitting raids that leave the group less vulnerable to Israeli airstrikes and intelligence penetration. Its use of first-person-view drones – drones using a live video feed from an onboard camera – to attack Israeli forces in southern Lebanon showcased the effectiveness of inexpensive technology, even as the movement has lost its more sophisticated capabilities. An Iranian expert with ties to both the Revolutionary Guards and Hizbollah told Crisis Group that Qods Force commanders have been directly involved in this revamping, including efforts to work through smaller units and help Hizbollah fighters adopt more agile tactics. Deterrence Moves Closer to Home, but the Axis Remains Important These changes reflect a broader reassessment of Iran’s deterrence posture. Its earlier approach heavily relied on the concept of “ forward defence ” ensured by regional partners, supplemented by the threat of direct retaliation from its own territory. The “axis of resistance” gave the Islamic Republic strategic depth , discouraging its adversaries from attacking it and keeping conflict distant from its borders. Only if that first layer of protection were to fail were Iranian missiles and drones to be used to shoot back. The past three years of war have starkly exposed the limits inherent in this arrangement. Iran’s regional network did not prevent direct attacks on the country – whether the major exchanges with Israel in 2024, the surprise Israeli attack in June 2025 or the more substantial confrontation with the U.S. and Israel beginning in February. As the deterrence value of axis partners dropped, Tehran was compelled to place greater weight on its own capabilities: missiles, drones and geographical leverage. If military setbacks have transformed the role played by the axis, they have not eliminated its utility to Iran. Yet, if military setbacks have transformed the role played by the axis, they have not eliminated its utility to Iran. Though the axis as a whole no longer serves as the primary foundation of Iran’s deterrence, decision-makers in Tehran believe that certain partners can play important roles in particular circumstances as they magnify Iran’s own capabilities and geographical leverage. Their experience during the present conflict with the U.S. has only bolstered this conviction. The Houthis have attained particular importance in the Islamic Republic’s thinking, which helps explain reports that Tehran has provided them with both guidance and military assistance. Tehran’s efforts in July to establish direct flights to Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen illustrated the multidimensional nature of this support: the flights both challenged restrictions imposed by Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Saudi Arabia on Houthi rule and reportedly carried Revolutionary Guards commanders, military advisers and missile- and drone-related equipment. Hizbollah, too, has retained its usefulness for Tehran. The movement attacked Israel following February’s U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, forcing Israel to contend with an additional front and placing further demands on its air defences. True, that supporting role was a far cry from the crucial deterrent function the movement was intended to play, a reflection of its diminished capabilities. Iranian officials have nevertheless continued to frame their confrontation with the U.S. and Israel as extending to Iran’s Middle East partners, Hizbollah in particular. In June, in a remarkable role reversal, Iran launched missiles at Israel in response to its campaign against Hizbollah, thereby marshalling its own forces in defence of its partner rather than the other way around. Moreover, it conditioned its acceptance of the (short-lived) 17 June memorandum of understanding halting hostilities with the U.S. on cessation of Israeli attacks in Lebanon: the opening clause explicitly included Lebanon in the ceasefire and affirmed Lebanese sovereignty and territorial integrity. Israel persisted with its offensive, however, including at Ali al-Taher , a strategic Hizbollah position in southern Lebanon where Israel besieged (and, in mid-September, demolished) an underground command and weapons complex. To Iranian officials, who had reportedly sent warnings that any such act would provoke a “forceful” response, the demolition was a reminder that Iranian threats of renewed missile attacks were an insufficient deterrent. Still, Iran’s stance showcased its commitment to axis members whose military utility has faded but not been erased. Decades of institutional ties, ideological affinity and investment help explain Iran’s approach. Decades of institutional ties, ideological affinity and investment help explain Iran’s approach. According to Iranian experts interviewed by Crisis Group, several members of the security establishment regard Hizbollah’s survival in particular as being closely tied to Iran’s own security, giving the relationship a significance that extends beyond the movement’s immediate military capabilities. This outlook has surfaced in public debates. In a January 2025 interview published by Iran’s Strategic Council on Foreign Relations, former diplomat Hadi Seyyed Afghahi argued that pressure on militant groups in Iraq, Lebanon and Yemen was aimed at “Iran and, more generally, the Shiites of the region”. Therefore, Tehran could not remain indifferent to these groups’ fate. Likewise, in December 2025, Ali Samadzadeh , an analyst with close ties to the regime, argued that Iran should be prepared to intervene militarily if Israel attacked Hizbollah, describing an assault on Lebanon as a prelude to renewed war with Iran. Defending regional partners, in this view, is part and parcel of protecting Iran itself. In short, where Tehran regards a partner as key to its own security, the fact that the partner has been weakened arguably – and perhaps paradoxically – provides Iran with added reason to intervene on its behalf. Efforts to curb Iranian influence by targeting allied groups may therefore draw Tehran into conflicts – a marked departure from the role these groups once played in shielding the Islamic Republic from direct involvement in hostilities. The extent of Iranian involvement is likely to depend on the particular relationship in question and the risks and costs inherent in intervention. But the bottom line is that its partners’ diminished military capabilities will not necessarily reduce Iran’s exposure to, or participation in, their respective conflicts. A Shifting Picture After three years of hostilities involving Iran’s partners and, since February, Iran itself, the “axis of resistance” is neither down nor out, but it is not what it once was, either in the function it serves or in Tehran’s relationship to its various members. The changes have been manifold. First, some of its members’ military capabilities have been significantly degraded. Secondly, direct confrontation with the U.S. and Israel has revealed the groups’ limited deterrent value and their inability to keep conflict away from Iranian territory. Finally, and partly as a result of their lessened status, they have come under growing domestic political, economic and security pressure, hindering their ability to directly participate in confrontations involving the Islamic Republic. These changes do not rule out these groups’ continued close operational ties to Tehran; nor do they mean an end to Iran’s commitment to their protection. But, together, they constrain the groups’ freedom of action. As a result, the focus of the Islamic Republic’s strategic doctrine has pivoted from allied non-state actors toward its own capabilities. This adjustment undoubtedly has preserved Iran’s ability to project power in its neighbourhood. But it does not come without serious risk, insofar as it has led Tehran to more directly bear the costs and dangers of confrontation. The Islamic Republic may well find ways to manage the consequences of its partners’ weakened clout by coming to their aid when they are endangered, giving them breathing space to regroup and using its own military assets to deter its foes, including by ensuring that others – notably Gulf Arab states – suffer the consequences of Middle East war. In so doing, Iran hopes to discourage future attacks. But this approach also risks deepening hostility among its neighbours, potentially encouraging closer security cooperation among Iran’s adversaries and heightening the very pressures Tehran seeks to reduce. Vietnam: Free Abducted Democracy Group Activists. Click to expand Image Nguyen Duc Thuan (left) and Tran Hiep. © Private (Bangkok) – The Vietnamese authorities should immediately release three activists associated with the overseas Viet Tan organization who went missing in Cambodia, and drop all charges against them, Human Rights Watch said today. The authorities should also grant Norwegian and Australian consular officials and family members immediate access to the detained men. The Vietnamese police claim that Nguyen Duc Thuan, a Norwegian citizen; Tran Hiep (also known as Ho Pham Hiep Huy), an Australian citizen; and Thai Cong Truong Son are members of the outlawed Viet Tan organization and attempted to use fake documents to cross the border from Cambodia to Vietnam on September 18, 2026. The men’s relatives say they never attempted to enter Vietnam. The police announced that they have charged the three men with “terrorism” under article 299 of the penal code for their association with Viet Tan and with forgery of seals and documents under article 341. Viet Tan is an overseas political organization that advocates for democratic change in Vietnam. It contends that the men were abducted in Cambodia. “The apparent abduction and detention of the foreign nationals raises many questions about the roles of both the Vietnamese and Cambodian governments,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The Norwegian and Australian governments should press the Vietnamese authorities to grant them immediate access to their nationals and to drop baseless charges against them.” Nguyen Duc Thuan and Tran Hiep flew to Phnom Penh on September 15 and were reportedly in regular contact with family members outside of Cambodia until the morning of September 18, after which neither could be reached. Both men missed other scheduled appointments in Cambodia and the flight they had booked to leave Cambodia on September 19; they have not been heard from since. Their luggage and other effects except phones and passports were found in their hotel rooms in Cambodia. Nguyen Duc Thuan requires daily insulin injections for diabetes and medical attention for kidney problems. As of October 11, neither the Australian nor Norwegian embassy had been granted access to the detained men. The Vietnamese police claimed that the three men crossed the border into Vietnam at Tay Ninh province, and that “Nguyen Duc Thuan was carrying two fake Vietnamese citizen identification cards” under a fake name and a Norwegian passport under his real name. They said that Ho Pham Hiep Huy “was carrying an Australian passport in the name of Tran Hiep.” The police statement does not describe Thai Cong Truong Son’s identification. On October 7, Cambodia’s Ministry of Interior issued a statement saying it had confirmed that Nguyen Duc Thuan and Tran Hiep had entered Cambodia but had not recorded their exit. And said it “categorically” denied any involvement in handing over the men to the Vietnamese authorities. In the 1980s, Viet Tan had engaged in armed resistance against Vietnam’s communist government. Viet Tan relaunched in 2004 as a political party committed to nonviolent change, but the Vietnamese authorities have arrested and imprisoned Viet Tan members. In 2016, Vietnam officially labeled Viet Tan a “terrorist group.” In 2019, an Australian member of Viet Tan, Chau Van Kham, and his colleagues Nguyen Van Vien and Tran Van Quyen were arrested in Vietnam and sentenced to 12, 11, and 10 years, respectively, for their involvement with Viet Tan on terrorism-related charges. Their trial lasted only 4.5 hours, suggesting that the verdict was pre-determined. The activities listed in the government’s charges against Chau Van Kham and attributed to Viet Tan, such as making travel arrangements to Vietnam, organizing leaflets for protests, expanding the Viet Tan’s network, writing articles, and sending people abroad for IT training, do not constitute acts of terrorism. In 2022, the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention issued an opinion stating that “the deprivation of liberty of [Viet Tan member] Chau Van Kham … is arbitrary.” Vietnam released Chau Van Kham in July 2023 and repatriated him to Australia. His Vietnamese fellow activists Nguyen Van Vien and Tran Van Quyen are still serving long prison sentences. In 2018, the Vietnamese police arrested Le Quoc Binh in Binh Dinh province and accused him of participating in Viet Tan and smuggling weapons from Cambodia into Vietnam to “carry out terrorist activities.” Viet Tan rejected the accusation, calling it “a ridiculous fabrication.” The then-public security minister and current Vietnamese president, To Lam, praised the police for arresting Le Quoc Binh. Later accounts in government media of his trial and conviction on charges of terrorism and illegal possession of weapons dropped all mention of Viet Tan. In May 2026, the Vietnamese police arrested Le Thanh Son and Nguyen Thanh Hung in Dong Thap province for their alleged affiliation with Viet Tan and charged them with “carrying out activities that aim to overthrow the people’s administration” under article 109 of the penal code. Also in May, the police reportedly detained, interrogated and beat a former political prisoner, Huynh Truong Ca, and forced him to admit that he was a member of Viet Tan, which he denied. After Huynh Truong Ca fled, police detained his family members, interrogated them on his whereabouts, and intimidated and pressured them to denounce him. In recent years, the Vietnamese authorities have stepped up transnational repression—government efforts to silence dissent by targeting dissidents and critics outside their territory. They have pressured other governments, including Thailand and Cambodia, to return Vietnamese citizens who fled Vietnam out of fear of arbitrary arrest, torture, or imprisonment. Vietnamese security forces have abducted Vietnamese citizens in Germany and Thailand, including Trinh Xuan Thanh, Truong Duy Nhat, and Duong Van Thai. In the past year, courts in Vietnam put on trial in absentia Vietnamese nationals who live overseas, convicting and sentencing them to long prison terms, including Le Trung Khoa, Nguyen Van Dai, Doan Bao Chau, Dinh Yum, Siu Di, and Dang Thi Hue. Since the trials, the police have issued numerous warnings and fined Vietnamese citizens for interacting with those convicted in absentia. Activists from Vietnam and Thailand have been forcibly disappeared in Cambodia in cases of suspected transnational repression. “Campaigning for democracy and pluralism is not a crime,” Pearson said. “The Vietnamese government should release Nguyen Duc Thuan, Tran Hiep, and Thai Cong Truong Son and end its practice of transnational repression.”

Libya: Eastern Authorities Carry Out Wave of Executions. Click to expand Image Military leader of Eastern Libya, Khalifa Haftar (center), attends a conference in Sabha, Libya, September 5, 2024. © 2024 Khaled Nasraoui/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Photo (Beirut) – The Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), which controls eastern and southern Libya, has executed at least 31 people since late August 2026 following grossly unfair military trials, Human Rights Watch said today. These are the first known executions in Libya since 2010, with at least 50 more people in Gernada military prison at imminent risk of execution. On August 23, the LAAF military prosecutor announced that 10 people had been executed by firing squad after being convicted of murder and terrorism-related offenses. Human rights groups have documented a total of at least 31 executions as of September 10. The LAAF, led by General Khalifa Haftar, should immediately halt all executions and impose a moratorium on the death penalty, Human Rights Watch said. “The Libyan Arab Armed Forces are putting people to death after secret trials built on confessions allegedly extracted through torture, in courts that Libya’s own Supreme Court has said should not be trying civilians,” said Bassam Khawaja, deputy Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “Every execution carried out under these conditions is an irreversible injustice and every government with influence over the LAAF should be pressing hard to stop the next one.” Many of those executed had been arrested in the cities of Derna and Benghazi during or after the armed conflict between the LAAF and opposing armed groups between 2014 and 2018. Between 2018 and 2021, military courts in eastern Libya convicted hundreds of civilians in secret trials targeting real or perceived critics of the LAAF, sentencing at least 22 to death. According to Amnesty International, many of the sentences were based on confessions allegedly extracted under torture by the Internal Security Agency, an LAAF-affiliated armed group. At least two death sentences were reduced to life in prison on appeal by a higher military court in 2019, yet the defendants were put to death this year regardless. The executions also went ahead despite a November 2025 ruling by the constitutional chamber of Libya’s Supreme Court that Law No. 4/2017 is unconstitutional insofar as it grants military courts jurisdiction to try civilians for terrorism and crimes against the state. Local human rights groups said that the military trials violated defendants’ due process rights. They were held in secret and without prior notice. Defendants’ families, journalists, and human rights organizations were not allowed to attend. Several defendants were denied lawyers of their choice and those who did have their own lawyers were refused visits before and during trial and could not speak with them privately. They were apparently not allowed to present their cases in court or examine the evidence against them. The verdicts were handed down without providing the defendants or their attorneys with written and reasoned judgments. Trying civilians in military courts is incompatible with the right to a fair trial under human rights law and such trials violate the right to be tried before an independent and impartial tribunal. In Libya, military prosecutors are often not qualified to investigate civilians and they lack independence. The military prosecutors and judges in eastern Libya are themselves affiliated with the LAAF or allied armed groups. Families of defendants were not notified in advance that the executions would take place. The authorities refused to hand over the bodies of those executed, asked relatives to confirm the identities of the dead, then buried them without families present and warned relatives not to hold funerals. Secret executions and denying families a last visit violate international law, including by inflicting severe mental suffering on those executed and their relatives in breach of the absolute prohibition of torture and other ill-treatment. Libya remains split between two rival authorities. The Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU), which is internationally recognized, controls the west, alongside affiliated security agencies and armed groups. The LAAF and affiliated forces and militias control the east and south. Both sides operate with near-total impunity. The United Nations and the GNU condemned the executions. Governments that fund, train, and legitimize the LAAF have real leverage, and a responsibility to use it, publicly and privately, to press LAAF leaders to halt all executions, Human Rights Watch said. Libya’s justice sector is fragmented and deeply polarized. Human Rights Watch has previously documented outdated and repressive legislation, a lack of fair trial rights, and rampant due process violations. Unaccountable militias control prisons that are only nominally under state ministries. Libyan authorities in both the east and west should restrict the jurisdiction of military courts to military offenses committed by military personnel and stop trying civilians in military courts altogether. They should promptly review all cases of civilians wrongfully detained and prosecuted before military courts and provide effective remedies, including release, transfer to civilian courts, or retrial in line with international fair trial standards, with acknowledgment of time served. Human Rights Watch opposes the death penalty in all countries and under all circumstances because it is inherently inhumane, uniquely cruel and irreversible, and universally plagued by arbitrariness, prejudice, and error. Ninety-two countries have ratified a protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights that requires the abolition of the death penalty, recognizing that capital punishment violates the right to life and the prohibition of cruel, inhuman, or degrading punishment. Libya should abolish the death penalty and until then enact a moratorium on all executions. “Libya went more than 15 years without an execution, and the LAAF has shattered that moratorium in a matter of weeks,” Khawaja said. “The lives of at least 50 more people now depend on whether Haftar’s forces, and the governments that back them, choose to stop this.”

European Governments Fall Short on Reparatory Justice. Click to expand Image Secretary-General António Guterres addresses the 55th session of the Human Rights Council in Geneva, Switzerland, February 26, 2024. © 2024 Elma Okic/UN Photo A United Nations Human Rights Council resolution on October 7 calling for concrete action against systemic racism should have been an opportunity for governments to demonstrate their commitment to racial justice. Instead, the United Kingdom called for a vote, breaking from last year’s consensus on the annually tabled resolution. Citing concerns about the applicability of international law to establish responsibility and accountability for colonial harm, the UK objected to language on reparations and then abstained from the vote; European Union members of the Council also abstained. Regardless, the resolution passed with 30 votes in favor, 17 abstentions, and none against. The loss of last year’s consensus reveals the gap between the UK and other European governments’ stated dedication to combat racism and their actual political willingness to address its historical roots. European governments have present-day obligations to tackle racial discrimination and provide effective remedies. The International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination requires states, including the UK, to ensure just and adequate reparation for harm resulting from racial discrimination. The experts who monitor this treaty earlier this year set out clear legal guidance on states’ obligations for such reparation. Enslavement and colonialism helped establish racial inequalities, the consequences of which persist today. Human Rights Watch has documented systemic racism, including racial profiling and barriers to economic and social rights in Europe. Reparatory justice is essential to confronting these enduring harms. Jamaica’s pursuit of an advisory opinion from the Judicial Committee of the UK’s Privy Council underscores the importance of examining governments’ legal arguments. Its petition asks whether the enslavement of Africans was lawful under English and international law, and whether the UK owes a reparatory remedy. Next month’s Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda offers another opportunity to change course. King Charles’s forthcoming Caribbean visit will, apparently, include an acknowledgement of Britain’s involvement in enslavement, although Buckingham Palace says decisions on reparations and formal apologies rest with the UK government. The UK and other European governments should engage meaningfully with African and Caribbean initiatives and affected communities to develop reparatory measures for the harms they were and are responsible for. These measures can include, according to UN principles, compensation, restitution, rehabilitation, acknowledgment of wrongdoing and reforms to prevent recurrence. Affected communities should shape the process and its outcomes. The United Nations Human Rights Council resolution calls on governments to move “from rhetoric to reality.” Those that are serious about ending systemic racism should embrace reparatory justice as part of that work.

French High School Student Protests Met with Excessive Force. Click to expand Image Students raise their hands in front of police officers as they demonstrate outside Sciences Po during a protest over school overcrowding and decay in Paris, France, October 7, 2026. © 2026 Tom Nicholson/Getty Images Images from ongoing student protests in France of heavily armed riot police using tear gas, stun grenades, batons, rubber bullets, and rough restraint techniques on children have sparked national and international concern. High schoolers across France have taken to the streets since September 21 frustrated with the government’s continued under-investment in their education, which has resulted in a shortage of teachers, too large classes, and inadequate school buildings. While schools have been blockaded and some protesters have engaged in violence, the protests have been overwhelmingly peaceful. Police use of force in response to the protests has resulted in serious injuries to children, including a 15-year-old boy who lost a hand to an explosive police stun grenade and a 14-year-old boy whose jaw shattered from a police tear-gas canister fired at close range. The government announced a temporary suspension of the use of stun grenades. Police have reportedly detained more than 6,800 people since the demonstrations started; with apparently 86 percent of them, children. Authorities have also reportedly opened 36 internal investigations into allegations of police misconduct. But internal reviews in France rarely translate into real accountability. Police use of excessive force during protests is not new in France. Human Rights Watch documented severe injuries caused by police during the 2018 “Yellow Vest” movement. And 2023’s pension reform protests and environmental demonstrations were also marked by such use of force. The current student protests began in schools in working-class neighborhoods, where racialized young people constantly experience and fear police harassment and state violence. Instead of addressing persistent problems with police using excessive force, the government is seeking to strengthen law enforcement’s right to use force. Under consideration since early 2026, a bill proposes to grant officers a “presumption of legality” when using their firearms. Rights groups warn the changes risk lowering the threshold for police to resort to use of firearms and shielding police from judicial scrutiny. French authorities should stop treating peacefully protesting children as a danger that needs to be neutralized. Instead, the government should uphold its obligations to protect children and their right to protest and listen to the demands of young people on the streets. To restore trust, the government should also thoroughly and promptly investigate all incidents of police use of force and end police tactics and reform the powers that foster police violence.

Kazakhstan Women Need Action on Domestic Violence. Click to expand Image Participants at the international Women's Day rally in Almaty, Kazakhstan, March 8, 2022. © 2022 Stanislav Beketov During its October 6 review by the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), Kazakhstan pledged new legislation to make domestic violence a standalone crime – a timely commitment. Now the government should turn words into action. On September 23, Zhazira Adauova, a mother of two, died after her ex-husband stabbed her 16 times in Astana, Kazakhstan’s capital. Zhazira’s family told the media she had repeatedly reported threats and violence to police. Four former police officers are under investigation for alleged negligence in handling her case. Elvira Erkebayeva, from western Kazakhstan, endured two decades of domestic violence, including having boiling water thrown in her face. Instead of protecting her and holding her former husband accountable, authorities prosecuted Elvira in 2025 for allegedly conspiring to murder him because she wanted to “find a firearm.” As in manyother cases, Kazakh authorities failed to protect women who sought protection against further violence, even when they had obtained multiple protection orders. Perpetrators are often held accountable only after killing their victims. Kazakhstan no longer has a dedicated law on domestic violence, and the latest reforms still did not establish domestic violence as a standalone criminal offense. The 2009 Law on Prevention of Domestic Violence was repealed by the Law on Prevention of Offences, which entered into force in March addresses domestic violence within a broader prevention framework. The Kazakh delegation claimed during its CEDAW review that “enforcing zero tolerance for violence had become … the cornerstone of ongoing reforms,” and that in 2024 Kazakhstan had “intensified legal accountability for domestic … violence.” Yet CEDAW experts rightly questioned the effectiveness of existing measures, and the Committee’s Rapporteur for Kazakhstan underscored that domestic violence is still not a standalone criminal offence. Under CEDAW and the Committee’s General Recommendation No. 35, states must prevent, investigate, prosecute, and ensure accountability for gender-based violence. Kazakhstan should adopt reforms to make domestic violence a standalone offence, strengthen and improve enforcement of the protection order mechanism, ensure interventions are effective and perpetrators held accountable, and guarantee survivors’ access to justice and services. Kazakhstan’s international partners should press for these reforms. Accountability after a woman is dead is no substitute for timely protection and prevention. Kazakh authorities need to ensure that women in Kazakhstan receive meaningful protection and assistance before violence escalates or turns fatal.
